conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.front: Classify the causes of bowel obstruction by wall location (intraluminal, intramural, extramural).
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.back: Intraluminal: gallstone ileus, foreign body, faecal impaction. Intramural: cancer, Crohn's/diverticular stricture, intussusception. Extramural: adhesions, hernias, peritoneal mets, volvulus.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.front: What are the cardinal four symptoms of bowel obstruction?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.back: Colicky/crampy abdominal pain; vomiting (bilious/green); abdominal distension; absolute constipation (no stool or flatus).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.front: What examination findings occur in bowel obstruction, and which is a red flag?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.back: Surgical scars, hernia, cachexia; signs of hypovolaemia (third-spacing); tympanic percussion with tinkling bowel sounds; and guarding/rebound → ischaemia developing (red flag).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.front: What bloods and gas results are relevant in bowel obstruction?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.back: FBC, CRP, U&E (hypokalaemia), LFT, lipase, G&S. ↑ urea:creatinine = dehydration/AKI. VBG: metabolic alkalosis (vomiting); raised lactate = ischaemia.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.front: What is the imaging modality of choice in bowel obstruction, and what does it show?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.back: CT abdo-pelvis + IV contrast — the modality of choice; shows site, cause, ischaemia, mets. Erect CXR shows pneumoperitoneum. Gastrografin at 24h: if no improvement, contrast not reaching the colon ≈ needs surgery.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.front: Compare SBO vs LBO on AXR diameter and location.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.back: Diameter: SBO >3 cm; LBO >6 cm (caecum >9 cm). Location: SBO central; LBO peripheral/frame.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.front: How do mucosal folds distinguish SBO from LBO on AXR?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.back: SBO: valvulae conniventes — cross the entire lumen. LBO: haustra — do not cross the full lumen.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.front: What is the conservative "drip & suck" management of bowel obstruction?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.back: Drip: IV fluids + correct electrolytes (especially K+). Suck: NBM + NG tube (Ryle's) to decompress the stomach. Plus a urinary catheter, strict fluid balance, and Gastrografin at 24h. Adhesional SBO resolves conservatively in ~80%.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.front: What proportion of adhesional SBO resolves with conservative management?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.back: Approximately 80%.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.front: What are the surgical indications in bowel obstruction?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.back: Suspected ischaemia (guarding, rebound, ↑ lactate); closed-loop obstruction; an underlying cause needing surgery (tumour, hernia); failure of conservative management at 48h; and a "virgin abdomen" — no prior surgery → structural cause likely → early exploration.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.front: Why does a "virgin abdomen" with obstruction prompt early exploration?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.back: No prior surgery means adhesions are unlikely, so a structural cause is likely → early exploration.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.front: Summarise the commonest causes of SBO vs LBO.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.back: SBO = adhesions (commonest). LBO = malignancy (commonest).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.front: How common is colorectal cancer, what cell type, and what is the key process?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.back: The 4th most common UK cancer; arises from epithelial cells → adenocarcinoma. The key process is the adenoma–carcinoma sequence (normal mucosa → adenoma → cancer over ~10–15 years). 75% are sporadic.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.front: What is the key fork when colorectal cancer is inherited?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.back: Polyposis (FAP) vs non-polyposis (Lynch).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.front: Compare the gene and inheritance of FAP vs Lynch/HNPCC.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.back: FAP: APC (tumour suppressor), autosomal dominant. Lynch/HNPCC: DNA mismatch repair genes (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6), autosomal dominant.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.front: Compare the adenoma burden and course of FAP vs Lynch.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.back: FAP: yes — floods the large intestine with 100s–1000s of polyps; inevitable cancer usually <40. Lynch: no — tumours arise in isolation; increased CRC + other cancers (endometrial, ovarian, gastric).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.front: Compare the prophylaxis of FAP vs Lynch.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.back: FAP: panproctocolectomy. Lynch: surveillance colonoscopy.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.front: What is the memory hook for FAP vs Lynch?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.back: FAP = Floods with polyps, APC. Lynch = Lonely tumours (no polyps), mismatch repair.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.front: What is the molecular sequence of colorectal carcinogenesis?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.back: APC mutation (initiation) → KRAS activation → p53 loss (invasion).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.front: Why do right-sided colorectal cancers present late, and what is the hallmark?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.back: Right-sided (caecum/ascending) tumours have a wide lumen → present late. Hallmark: iron-deficiency anaemia, abdominal pain, palpable RIF mass.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.front: Why do left-sided colorectal cancers obstruct earlier, and what is the hallmark?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.back: Left-sided (descending/sigmoid/rectum) tumours have a narrow lumen → obstruct earlier. Hallmark: rectal bleeding, change in bowel habit, tenesmus, mucus PR.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.front: What are the key differentials for colorectal cancer?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.back: Diverticular disease (pain + habit change, same age — always exclude CRC); haemorrhoids (bright-red PR blood, no habit change/weight loss/anaemia); IBD (younger, bloody diarrhoea).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.front: What is the NHS bowel screening test, who is screened, and what did it replace?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.back: FIT test (faecal immunochemical test — measures human Hb) every 2 years, ages 50–74 (the programme has been extended down to age 50). FIT replaced gFOBT (which gave false positives from dietary red meat).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.front: What are the 2-week-wait referral criteria for colorectal cancer?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.back: ≥40 with unexplained weight loss AND abdominal pain; ≥50 with unexplained rectal bleeding; ≥60 with IDA OR change in bowel habit; positive FIT (any age).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.front: What does unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia warrant, and what does "top and tail" mean?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.back: Unexplained IDA → 2WW "top and tail" = colonoscopy + gastroscopy.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.front: What is the gold-standard diagnostic test for colorectal cancer, and what are the alternatives?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.back: Colonoscopy + biopsy — the gold standard. CT colonography if frail/colonoscopy intolerance. Flexible sigmoidoscopy if the only symptom is rectal bleeding.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.front: What investigations are used for staging colorectal cancer?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.back: CT chest-abdomen-pelvis — metastases + local invasion (all CRC). MRI rectum — rectal cancers only; depth of invasion, mesorectal fascia. Endoanal USS — early rectal (T1/T2). CEA — NOT diagnostic; used to monitor recurrence.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.front: What is the role of CEA in colorectal cancer?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.back: NOT diagnostic — used to monitor recurrence.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.front: What do the TNM T-stages (T1–T4) correspond to in depth?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.back: T1: submucosa. T2: muscularis propria. T3: subserosa/perirectal fat. T4a/b: through serosa / into adjacent organs.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.front: What do the Dukes stages A–D correspond to, with their 5-year survival?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.back: A: confined to bowel wall (~90%). B: through wall, no nodes (~65%). C: lymph node involvement (~30%). D: distant metastases (<10%).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.front: What operations are used for right-sided and left-sided colon cancers?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.back: Caecum/ascending/proximal transverse → right hemicolectomy (ileo-colic anastomosis). Distal transverse/descending → left hemicolectomy (colo-colic anastomosis).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.front: What operations are used for sigmoid and upper rectal cancers?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.back: Sigmoid → high anterior resection (colo-rectal anastomosis). Upper rectum → anterior resection (TME) (colo-rectal anastomosis).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.front: What operations are used for low rectal cancers, and how does the distance from the anus decide?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.back: Low rectum >5 cm → low anterior resection (LAR) — sphincter-sparing (colo-rectal anastomosis ± defunctioning stoma). Low rectum <5 cm → abdominoperineal resection (APR) — permanent end colostomy.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.front: What is the emergency operation for obstructing colorectal cancer?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.back: Hartmann's — end colostomy (reversible).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.front: Why is radiotherapy used only for rectal cancer and not colon cancer?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.back: Radiotherapy = rectal cancer only (neoadjuvant, pre-op). The rectum is extraperitoneal — safe to irradiate. The colon is intraperitoneal and mobile — cannot be safely irradiated.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.front: What is a stoma, and what is the decisive fork in understanding it?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.back: An artificial opening of the bowel or urinary system onto the abdominal surface; a bag collects waste, bypassing distal portions of the tract. The decisive fork = what's brought out and why (defunctioning vs permanent after resection).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.front: What is brought out and what is the output in a colostomy vs ileostomy?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.back: Colostomy: colon is brought out; output is more solid (water already reabsorbed). Ileostomy: ileum (terminal small bowel) is brought out; output is more liquid (reabsorption occurs downstream in the colon, which is bypassed).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.front: Compare the profile and typical site of a colostomy vs ileostomy.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.back: Colostomy: flat to skin (solid output is not irritant); typical site LIF. Ileostomy: spouted (liquid is irritant; must drain clear of skin); typical site RIF.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.front: What is the memory hook for colostomy vs ileostomy?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.back: Ileostomy = Irritant liquid → needs a spout, sits in RIF. Colostomy = solid, flat, LIF.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.front: How is an end stoma made, and what is its purpose?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.back: The proximal cut end is brought to the skin; the distal end is sutured closed inside the abdomen. Purpose: after resection of a bowel segment.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.front: How is a loop stoma made, and what is its purpose?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.back: Bowel is partially opened and folded → two openings side-by-side. Purpose: to defunction a distal anastomosis (let it heal).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.front: Compare the reversibility of an end stoma vs a loop stoma.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.back: End stoma: sometimes reversible (if the distal end is preserved). Loop stoma: yes — reversed at 6–8 weeks.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.front: What is an end colostomy, when is it permanent, and where does it sit?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.back: Permanent after APR — the rectum + anus are removed, so reversal is impossible. It sits in the lower left abdomen (LIF).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.front: What is an end ileostomy, when is it permanent, and what is the alternative?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.back: Permanent after panproctocolectomy (IBD, FAP). Sits in the RIF. Alternative: a J-pouch (ileo-anal anastomosis) — avoids a permanent stoma.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.front: What is a gastrostomy used for, and how is it fitted?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.back: An artificial connection between the stomach and abdominal wall — it delivers feed directly when oral nutrition is not possible (feeding, not draining). PEG (percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy) is fitted endoscopically.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.front: What are the indications for a gastrostomy?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.back: Neurological dysphagia (stroke, MND) and head/neck cancer.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.front: What is a urostomy (ileal conduit), and what is its indication?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.back: Urine bypasses the bladder and urethra (the ureters are anastomosed to the ileal conduit). Indication: after cystectomy (bladder removal). It is spouted (urine is irritant) and sited in the RIF.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.front: How is a urostomy (ileal conduit) constructed?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.back: 15–20 cm of ileum is isolated; the remaining bowel is re-anastomosed. The ureters are anastomosed to the isolated ileal segment, and the distal end is brought to the skin as a stoma → urine drains into a bag.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.front: What are the skin/mechanical complications of stomas?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.back: Peristomal skin irritation (especially ileostomy/urostomy), granulomas (raised red lumps at the stoma margin), parastomal hernia (bowel herniates through the defect), prolapse (bowel telescopes through), retraction (sinks below skin — leak risk), and stenosis/obstruction.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.front: What is a high-output ileostomy, and what does it lead to?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.back: It causes dehydration + electrolyte loss (Na+, K+, Mg2+) → AKI. It is the key metabolic complication.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.front: What are the other functional/metabolic and psychosocial complications of stomas?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.back: Malabsorption, nutritional deficiency, constipation (colostomies), and body image issues, depression, and adjustment difficulties (psychosocial).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.front: What is Clostridioides difficile (C. diff) infection, and how does it arise?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.back: Pseudomembranous colitis caused by toxin-mediated mucosal damage after broad-spectrum antibiotics suppress normal gut flora, allowing C. diff overgrowth.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.front: What is the core framing for suspecting C. diff?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.back: "Recent broad-spectrum antibiotics + new diarrhoea, especially in hospital = C. diff until proven otherwise." Always exclude C. diff toxin in every IBD flare with diarrhoea before escalating immunosuppression.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.front: What are the "4 Cs" — the causative antibiotics for C. diff?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.back: Cephalosporins (the leading cause), ciprofloxacin (fluoroquinolones), clindamycin, and co-amoxiclav.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.front: What additional risk factors predispose to C. diff?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.back: PPIs (↓ gastric acid barrier), advanced age, hospitalisation/healthcare exposure, and immunosuppression.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.front: What is the mechanism of C. diff infection?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.back: Antibiotics → flora suppression → C. diff overgrows → toxin A (enterotoxin) + toxin B (cytotoxin) → mucosal damage → pseudomembranous colitis.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.front: What is the typical clinical presentation of C. diff infection?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.back: Profuse, foul-smelling diarrhoea; diffuse abdominal pain/cramping; fever; raised WCC (leukocytosis); dehydration; and recent antibiotics/hospitalisation.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.front: What are the severe / life-threatening features of C. diff infection, and the key imaging clue?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.back: Toxic megacolon (colon >6 cm + systemic sepsis, shared with UC), ileus (silent abdomen), perforation, and hypotension/shock. Imaging clue: thumbprinting (mucosal oedema) on AXR.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.front: How is mild C. diff defined and treated?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.back: Normal WCC, <3 stools/day, no systemic upset → oral vancomycin.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.front: How is moderate C. diff defined and treated?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.back: WCC <15 ×10⁹/L, 3–5 stools/day → oral vancomycin.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.front: How is severe C. diff defined and treated?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.back: WCC >15 ×10⁹/L, with temp >38.5°C or creatinine ↑>50% → oral vancomycin ± IV metronidazole.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.front: How is life-threatening C. diff defined and treated?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.back: Any WCC, with hypotension, ileus, or toxic megacolon → oral vancomycin + IV metronidazole ± colectomy.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.front: What is the key severity threshold in C. diff that should prompt early escalation?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.back: WCC >15 or AKI = severe — escalate early.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.front: What is the gold-standard diagnostic test for C. diff, and what does it detect?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.back: Stool C. diff toxin (CDT) — the gold standard; detects toxin A & B.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.front: What is the role of GDH antigen testing in C. diff, and how is a positive result handled?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.back: GDH antigen — a sensitive screening test; if positive, confirm with the toxin assay.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.front: What is the critical diagnostic nuance regarding GDH+/toxin- results?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.back: GDH+/toxin- = colonisation, not infection. You must detect toxin — treating colonisation is a recognised error.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.front: What severity markers are used in C. diff, and what does each flag?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.back: FBC — WCC (severity threshold); U&E/creatinine — AKI flags severity; CRP — elevated in active disease; AXR — toxic megacolon, thumbprinting, ileus if severe; CT abdomen — if perforation suspected.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.front: What is the first step and 1st-line treatment for a first episode of C. diff?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.back: Stop the offending antibiotic (where possible). 1st-line: oral vancomycin 125 mg QDS × 10 days.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.front: What is the 2nd-line treatment for a first episode of C. diff?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.back: Oral fidaxomicin 200 mg BD × 10 days.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.front: How is severe and life-threatening C. diff treated in the first-episode ladder?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.back: Severe: oral vancomycin 500 mg QDS + IV metronidazole. Life-threatening: the above + surgical review (colectomy).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.front: How is recurrent C. diff managed depending on timing?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.back: Within 12 weeks → oral fidaxomicin. After 12 weeks → oral vancomycin OR fidaxomicin. Multiple recurrences → Faecal Microbiota Transplant (FMT).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.front: What infection control measures are used for C. diff, and why is handwashing specific?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.back: Isolate in a single room with contact precautions; soap-and-water handwashing (C. diff spores resist alcohol gel); dedicated toilet; PPE (gloves + apron) for all contacts; and antibiotic stewardship — limit the 4 Cs.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.front: What is the updated guideline trap regarding first-line C. diff treatment?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.back: Metronidazole is NO LONGER first-line. Current NICE guidance: oral vancomycin = 1st-line. Older question banks still say metronidazole — know the current answer.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.front: What is diverticular disease, and where is it commonest?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.back: Outpouchings of colonic mucosa through weak points in the bowel wall, commonest in the sigmoid colon. It is a spectrum from silent pouches to life-threatening peritonitis.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.front: Define diverticulosis and its symptoms.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.back: Pouches present. Asymptomatic (an incidental finding).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.front: Define diverticular disease (the symptomatic stage) and its symptoms.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.back: Symptomatic pouches. Intermittent LIF pain and altered bowel habit.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.front: Define diverticulitis and its symptoms.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.back: Inflamed/infected pouches. LIF pain + systemic upset (fever, raised CRP).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.front: Define a diverticular bleed and how it presents.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.back: Vessel erosion. Presents as a painless, large-volume PR bleed.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.front: What is the key differential for diverticular disease, and how is IBD distinguished?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.back: Colorectal cancer is the key differential (same demographic — always exclude). IBD is distinguished by faecal calprotectin.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.front: Why do diverticula form?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.back: Low-fibre diet → harder stool → straining → ↑ intraluminal pressure; ageing bowel wall loses tensile strength; mucosa herniates through weak points where blood vessels penetrate the circular muscle (between the taenia coli).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.front: Why do diverticula never form in the rectum?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.back: The rectum has a complete outer longitudinal muscle layer and no taenia coli, so there are no weak points for herniation.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.front: Why do diverticula bleed, and what is the clinical significance?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.back: A vasa recta runs directly alongside each pouch (the same anatomical weak point). Erosion → painless, large-volume arterial PR bleed. It is the most common cause of significant lower GI haemorrhage in adults.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.front: What are the risk factors for diverticular disease?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.back: Low fibre (the key modifiable factor), high red meat, age, obesity, and smoking. NSAIDs/steroids increase perforation risk.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.front: What are the clinical features of acute diverticulitis?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.back: LIF pain (worse on movement), fever, anorexia, nausea, altered bowel habit ± PR bleeding, urinary symptoms (bladder irritation), LIF tenderness ± a palpable mass (abscess) on exam, and guarding/rebound → complicated (perforation).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.front: What distinguishes simple from complicated diverticulitis, and what analogy is used?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.back: Simple = inflammation only. Complicated = abscess, perforation, fistula, or obstruction. Described as "left-sided appendicitis" — same inflammatory-then-perforation logic, opposite side.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.front: What is the first-line imaging in diverticulitis, and what does it show?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.back: CT abdo-pelvis — bowel wall thickening, pericolonic fat stranding, abscess, free air (perforation). Erect CXR shows pneumoperitoneum if perforation is suspected.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.front: Why must colonoscopy never be done acutely in diverticulitis, and when is it done?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.back: Perforation risk. Scope after resolution (6–8 weeks) to exclude colorectal cancer.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.front: What bloods/tests are relevant in diverticulitis?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.back: FBC (raised WCC), CRP (elevated; guides severity), U&E (AKI in sepsis), G&S (if surgical intervention possible), faecal calprotectin (if IBD unclear), and urine dip (leucocytes ± haematuria from bladder irritation).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.front: What is the Hinchey classification of diverticulitis, and the management for stage 0/Ia?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.back: A staging system linking findings to management. Stage 0/Ia: mild/pericolic phlegmon → oral antibiotics (outpatient).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.front: What is the management for Hinchey stage Ib/II?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.back: Pericolic or pelvic abscess → IV antibiotics ± CT-guided drainage (if >5 cm).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.front: What is the management for Hinchey stages III and IV?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.back: Stage III: purulent peritonitis → surgery (Hartmann's procedure). Stage IV: faecal peritonitis → surgery (Hartmann's procedure).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.front: How is uncomplicated diverticulitis managed as an outpatient?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.back: Oral co-amoxiclav ≥5 days (cipro + metronidazole if pen-allergic) — though NICE NG147 advises antibiotics are not routinely needed if the patient is systemically well; paracetamol — avoiding NSAIDs (↑ perforation) and opioids (mask symptoms); clear fluids, rest, review at 48h; and colonoscopy 6–8 weeks post-resolution to exclude CRC.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.front: How is complicated diverticulitis managed on admission?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.back: NBM, IV fluids, analgesia; IV antibiotics (co-amoxiclav or pip-tazo); abscess >5 cm → CT-guided drainage; perforation/peritonitis → Hartmann's (sigmoid colectomy + end colostomy; ~50% reversible).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.front: How does a diverticular bleed (vascular) differ from diverticulitis (inflammatory)?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.back: Diverticulitis (inflammatory): LIF pain + fever, raised WCC/CRP, ± minor PR bleeding. Diverticular bleed (vascular): painless, large-volume, fresh PR bleed; no fever, no inflammatory response; usually self-limiting (80%).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.front: What is the management ladder for a diverticular bleed?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.back: Resuscitate → CT angiography (1st-line) → endoscopic haemostasis / embolisation → surgery if refractory.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.front: What are the acute complications of diverticular disease?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.back: Abscess (CT-guided drainage if >5 cm), perforation → peritonitis → Hartmann's, and haemorrhage.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.front: What is the commonest fistula in chronic diverticular disease, and how does it present?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.back: Colovesical fistula (commonest, in men) → pneumaturia, faecaluria, and recurrent UTIs.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.front: What are the other chronic complications (fistulae/stricture) of diverticular disease, and what do they all require?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.back: Colovaginal fistula → faeces/flatus per vagina; stricture → large bowel obstruction. All fistulae require surgery.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: What is IBD, and what are its two types?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: Recurrent inflammation of the GI tract. Two types: Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis (UC) — distinguished by distribution, depth, and pathological pattern.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: What does the NESTTS mnemonic capture about Crohn's disease?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: Non-bloody diarrhoea, Entire GI tract (mouth→anus), Skip lesions, Transmural (full thickness), Thick wall/strictures/fistulae, Smoking worsens.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: What are the key 'closeup' features of ulcerative colitis?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: Continuous (no skip), large bowel only (colon + rectum), only mucosa/submucosa, smoking protective, elevated cancer risk, ulcerations/pseudopolyps, and PSC association.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: Compare the distribution of Crohn's vs UC.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: Crohn's: mouth → anus; terminal ileum commonest; skip lesions. UC: rectum upward, continuous; never past the ileocaecal valve.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: Compare the depth of inflammation in Crohn's vs UC.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: Crohn's: transmural (full thickness). UC: mucosa/submucosa only.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: Compare the diarrhoea of Crohn's vs UC.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: Crohn's: non-bloody; weight loss prominent. UC: bloody + mucus; tenesmus, LLQ pain.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: Compare the histology of Crohn's vs UC.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: Crohn's: non-caseating granulomas, transmural inflammation, goblet cells preserved. UC: crypt abscesses, mucosal/submucosal inflammation, goblet cell depletion.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: Compare the endoscopy findings of Crohn's vs UC.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: Crohn's: cobblestone, deep ulcers, skip lesions. UC: pseudopolyps, continuous inflammation.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: Compare the radiology findings of Crohn's vs UC.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: Crohn's: Kantor's string sign, rose-thorn ulcers, fistulae. UC: lead-pipe colon, loss of haustra.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: How does smoking affect Crohn's vs UC?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: Crohn's: a risk factor (worsens disease). UC: protective (the counterintuitive classic).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: Compare the complications of Crohn's vs UC.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: Crohn's: fistulae, strictures, abscesses, obstruction; gallstones (↓bile acid reabsorption). UC: toxic megacolon, colorectal cancer, PSC.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: Compare the role of surgery in Crohn's vs UC.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: Crohn's: not curative — disease recurs (panenteric). UC: curative — panproctocolectomy removes the entire disease.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: What are the key discriminators that separate UC from Crohn's?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: Bloody = UC; non-bloody + weight loss = Crohn's; granulomas = Crohn's; crypt abscesses = UC; skip/transmural = Crohn's; continuous/mucosal = UC; smoking protects in UC, harms in Crohn's.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: What are the eye and skin extraintestinal manifestations of IBD?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: Eyes: uveitis, episcleritis. Skin: erythema nodosum (tender red nodules, shins) and pyoderma gangrenosum (a deep ulcerating skin lesion).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: What are the joint, hepatobiliary, and renal extraintestinal manifestations of IBD?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: Joints: arthralgia, ankylosing spondylitis/sacroiliitis (HLA-B27). Hepatobiliary: PSC especially with UC; gallstones in Crohn's (↓bile acid reabsorption from terminal ileum disease). Renal: oxalate renal stones in Crohn's (↑oxalate absorption due to fat malabsorption).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: What do bloods show in IBD?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: Anaemia, ↑WCC, ↑CRP/ESR (normal in IBS — the discriminator), ↓albumin (severe disease), and LFTs (PSC).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: What is the role of faecal calprotectin in IBD?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: The IBS vs IBD discriminator — raised in IBD (mucosal inflammation), normal in IBS.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: Why are stool cultures + C. difficile testing done in IBD?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: Always exclude an infectious cause of diarrhoea and C. difficile (especially if recent antibiotics) before confirming an IBD flare.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: What is the investigation of choice for IBD, and what are the cautions in severe colitis?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: Colonoscopy + biopsy is the investigation of choice for both. Flexi-sigmoidoscopy only in severe colitis (full colonoscopy → perforation risk). AXR in acute severe UC → exclude toxic megacolon (>6cm transverse colon).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: What imaging is used specifically in Crohn's disease?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: MRI small bowel / CT abdomen — to assess extent, fistulae, abscesses. Small bowel enema: rose-thorn ulcers, string sign.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: Define Crohn's disease and its commonest site.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: Transmural, skip-lesion inflammation affecting any part of the GI tract from mouth to anus. The terminal ileum is the commonest site. Fistulae, strictures, and abscesses are its distinctive complications.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: Describe the diarrhoea and weight loss features of Crohn's disease.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: Diarrhoea: chronic/intermittent, usually non-bloody; may be steatorrhoeic if terminal ileum involvement (↓fat absorption). Weight loss + malnutrition: malabsorption + anorexia + catabolism — a prominent feature distinguishing Crohn's from UC clinically.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: Describe the abdominal pain, perianal disease, and mouth ulcers of Crohn's.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: Abdominal pain: RIF pain (terminal ileum) mimics appendicitis; colicky, post-prandial if strictures. Perianal disease: fistulae, skin tags, fissures, abscesses — pathognomonic of Crohn's; may predate GI symptoms. Mouth ulcers: aphthous — reflect mouth-to-anus distribution; often the first/only sign in some patients.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: What is the 1st-line treatment to induce remission in Crohn's, and which agent is used for terminal ileal/right-sided disease?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: Steroids — oral prednisolone (mild-moderate); IV hydrocortisone (severe/hospitalised). Budesonide for terminal ileal/right-sided disease (topical effect, fewer systemic side effects).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: What steroid-sparing agent is added in Crohn's, and what must be checked before starting it?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: Azathioprine / mercaptopurine — a steroid-sparing immunosuppressant. Check TPMT activity before starting: TPMT deficiency → severe myelosuppression (a classic prescribing SBA).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: What biologic is used for refractory or fistulating Crohn's, and what must be done before starting?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: Infliximab (anti-TNF) — biologic therapy for refractory or fistulating disease. Also adalimumab, ustekinumab, vedolizumab. Screen for TB before starting.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: What is the preferred remission-induction option in children with Crohn's, and why?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: Enteral nutrition — preferred over steroids in children. Exclusive enteral nutrition (EEN) has equivalent efficacy to steroids with nutritional benefit and no steroid side effects.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: How is remission maintained in Crohn's disease?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: 1st-line: azathioprine/mercaptopurine — the backbone of maintenance; methotrexate if intolerant. 2nd-line: methotrexate (monitor LFTs, folate supplementation); anti-TNF biologics for persistent/severe.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: What are the surgical principles in Crohn's disease, and is surgery curative?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: Resect isolated/symptomatic disease (e.g. terminal ileal resection); treat strictures (balloon dilatation or stricturoplasty); perianal fistula → MRI + metronidazole ± seton + infliximab; abscess → I&D + antibiotics. Surgery does NOT cure Crohn's — disease recurs at new sites (panenteric).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: Describe fistulae as a complication of Crohn's disease.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: Transmural inflammation → tracks between loops (entero-enteric), bladder (enterovesical → pneumaturia), skin (enterocutaneous), or perianal. Pathognomonic of Crohn's.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: How do strictures/obstruction and gallstones arise in Crohn's?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: Strictures: fibrosis from repeated transmural inflammation → luminal narrowing → Kantor's string sign on contrast → bowel obstruction. Gallstones: terminal ileum disease → ↓bile-acid reabsorption → bile-acid pool depleted → bile becomes cholesterol-supersaturated → cholesterol gallstones.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: What malabsorption/nutritional complications occur in Crohn's?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: B12 deficiency (terminal ileum), fat-soluble vitamins, iron, folate, and oxalate renal stones.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: Define ulcerative colitis and its hallmark.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: Mucosal inflammation of the colon and rectum, continuous from the rectum upward, never extending past the ileocaecal valve. Bloody diarrhoea is the hallmark.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: Describe the clinical features of ulcerative colitis.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: Bloody diarrhoea + mucus is the hallmark — rectal bleeding + loose stool, with tenesmus (sensation of incomplete emptying), urgency, LLQ/central cramping pain. Systemic upset (severe): fever, tachycardia, weight loss, ↓Hb, ↑CRP/ESR, ↓albumin (Truelove-Witts severe criteria).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: What is the Truelove-Witts severity grading for UC?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: Mild: <4 stools/day, no systemic features. Moderate: 4–6 stools/day, minimal systemic features. Severe: >6 bloody stools/day, with fever, tachycardia, anaemia (Hb<10.5), ↑ESR (>30).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: What flare triggers should be avoided in ulcerative colitis?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: Stress, NSAIDs, antibiotics, and stopping smoking (smoking is protective — cessation can precipitate a flare).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: How is remission induced in mild-moderate ulcerative colitis?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: Aminosalicylates (mesalazine) 1st-line — oral ± rectal (suppository/enema); rectal only reaches the splenic flexure, so use oral if beyond the left colon. Steroids (oral prednisolone) 2nd-line.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: How is remission induced in severe ulcerative colitis (admit)?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: IV hydrocortisone 1st-line. No response by day 3–5 → IV ciclosporin or infliximab. LMWH (high VTE risk in active colitis). Colectomy if failing medical therapy. AXR to exclude toxic megacolon.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: How is remission maintained in ulcerative colitis?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: 1st-line: aminosalicylates — mesalazine oral ± rectal; monitor FBC (aminosalicylates → agranulocytosis: check FBC if fever/sore throat, same vigilance as carbimazole) and pancreatitis. After severe/frequent relapses: azathioprine/mercaptopurine (check TPMT); anti-TNF biologics (infliximab, vedolizumab) for refractory.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: What is the curative surgery for ulcerative colitis, and what are the options?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: Panproctocolectomy removes the entire diseased organ → cures UC. Options: permanent ileostomy (simpler, reliable); or ileoanal pouch (J-pouch) — a reservoir fashioned from ileum, anastomosed to anus, avoiding a permanent stoma but with risk of pouchitis.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: Describe toxic megacolon as a complication of UC.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: Colonic dilatation >6cm on AXR + systemic toxicity. Life-threatening. Emergency colectomy if medical therapy fails within 24–48h.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: Describe the colorectal cancer risk in UC and its surveillance.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: Increased risk with pancolitis and long disease duration (>10yr), and PSC. Surveillance colonoscopy every 1–5 years depending on risk.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: Describe primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) in UC.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: Stricturing of the biliary tree — the classic UC hepatic association. Raised ALP, increased cholangiocarcinoma risk.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.front: Describe anaemia as a complication of UC.
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.back: Chronic blood loss → iron-deficiency anaemia. Also anaemia of chronic disease (↑IL-6, ↓erythropoiesis).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.question: Which two dangerous mimics must always be excluded when assessing an anorectal complaint?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.answer: Colorectal cancer (bleeding) and Crohn's disease (fistulae/abscesses)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.explanation: The can't-miss dangerous mimics are colorectal cancer (bleeding) and Crohn's disease (fistulae/abscesses) — always exclude these.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.question: Which three triage questions split the anorectal disease group?
options: Painful or painless? Bleeding or discharge? Lump or no lump?
Acute or chronic? Internal or external? Reducible or not?
Fever or no fever? Anaemia or not? Weight loss or not?
Bright or dark blood? Mixed or surface? Mucus or not?
Male or female? Young or old? Hirsute or not?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.answer: Painful or painless? Bleeding or discharge? Lump or no lump?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.explanation: The triage fork is: painful or painless? bleeding or discharge? lump or no lump? These split the whole group.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.question: Which anorectal condition is characteristically painless (unless thrombosed) with bright red bleeding on the surface and a prolapsing lump?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.answer: Haemorrhoids
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.explanation: Haemorrhoids are painless (unless thrombosed) with bright red bleeding on the surface, mucus discharge and a prolapsing lump.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.question: Which condition presents with persistent discharge, mild or no pain, and an external opening?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.answer: Fistula-in-ano
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.explanation: Fistula-in-ano has mild/no pain, persistent discharge and an external opening on the triage table.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.question: Which examination is used specifically to assess haemorrhoids and fissures?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.answer: Proctoscopy
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.explanation: The shared exam approach is inspection, DRE (tone, masses, tenderness) and proctoscopy for haemorrhoids/fissure.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.question: What is the cryptoglandular basis linking perianal abscess and fistula-in-ano?
options: Hair penetrating the skin driving a foreign-body reaction
Splitting of the distal anal mucosa from hard stool
Enlargement of the anal vascular cushions
Chronic infection of the anal crypt glands — an abscess forms then discharges, leaving a tract (same process, acute vs chronic)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.answer: Chronic infection of the anal crypt glands — an abscess forms then discharges, leaving a tract (same process, acute vs chronic)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.explanation: Fistula formation occurs through chronic infection of the anal crypt glands — an abscess forms, then discharges pus via the skin, leaving a tract. It is the same cryptoglandular process, acute (abscess) vs chronic (fistula).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.question: Recurrent, complex or multiple perianal disease should prompt thinking about which underlying condition?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.answer: Crohn's disease (IBD)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.explanation: Perianal disease (especially fistulae + abscesses) is a classic Crohn's feature; recurrent/complex/multiple perianal disease should prompt thinking about IBD.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.question: What are haemorrhoids?
options: A split in the distal anal mucosa
A collection of pus from gland infection
Abnormal swelling/enlargement of the anal vascular cushions
An epithelial-lined tract to the skin
A hair-containing sinus in the natal cleft
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.answer: Abnormal swelling/enlargement of the anal vascular cushions
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.explanation: Haemorrhoids are abnormal swelling/enlargement of the anal vascular cushions, which normally help the sphincter maintain continence.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.question: At which clock positions (lithotomy) are the three haemorrhoidal cushions located?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.answer: 3, 7 and 11 o'clock
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.explanation: The three cushions sit at 3, 7 and 11 o'clock in the lithotomy position; peak age is 45–65.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.question: Why are internal haemorrhoids (above the dentate line) typically painless?
options: They are covered by keratinised skin
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.answer: They have visceral innervation
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.explanation: Internal haemorrhoids (above the dentate line) are painless because of visceral innervation and tend to prolapse and bleed; external ones (below the line) can be painful due to somatic innervation.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.question: A patient has haemorrhoids that prolapse on defecation but reduce spontaneously. What degree are these?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.answer: 2nd degree
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.explanation: 2nd-degree haemorrhoids prolapse on defecation and spontaneously reduce. 1st remain in the rectum, 3rd require digital reduction, and 4th are persistently prolapsed.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.question: Which haemorrhoid grade is persistently prolapsed and cannot be reduced?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.answer: 4th degree
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.explanation: 4th-degree haemorrhoids are persistently prolapsed; 3rd-degree prolapse but require digital reduction.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.question: Which feature best discriminates haemorrhoidal bleeding from colorectal cancer?
options: Haemorrhoidal blood is always dark and tarry
Haemorrhoidal blood is mixed through the stool
Haemorrhoidal blood is on the surface of the stool/on the paper, not mixed in
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.answer: Haemorrhoidal blood is on the surface of the stool/on the paper, not mixed in
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.explanation: Haemorrhoidal blood is on the surface of the stool or on the paper, not mixed in; blood mixed through the stool points to cancer.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.question: A large prolapsed haemorrhoid becomes acutely very painful with a purple/blue, oedematous, tense, tender mass. What has happened?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.answer: It has thrombosed
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.explanation: Large prolapsed haemorrhoids can thrombose, becoming very painful with an acute purple/blue, oedematous, tense, tender mass.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.question: Which management is appropriate for 1st/2nd-degree haemorrhoids that fail conservative measures?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.answer: Rubber-band ligation
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.explanation: 1st/2nd-degree haemorrhoids are treated with rubber-band ligation. HAL/THD is used for 2nd/3rd, and haemorrhoidectomy (Milligan-Morgan or stapled) for 3rd/4th.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.question: Why should opioid analgesia be avoided in haemorrhoids?
options: It worsens constipation and the underlying problem
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.answer: It worsens constipation and the underlying problem
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.explanation: Opioid analgesia should be avoided because it worsens constipation and the underlying problem.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.question: What is an anal fissure?
options: A split in the distal anal mucosa causing sharp pain on defecation and bleeding
Enlargement of the anal vascular cushions
A collection of pus from gland infection
An epithelial-lined tract to the skin
A hair-containing sinus in the natal cleft
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.answer: A split in the distal anal mucosa causing sharp pain on defecation and bleeding
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.explanation: An anal fissure is a split in the distal anal mucosa causing sharp anal pain on defecation and bleeding.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.question: What triad develops in a chronic (>6 weeks) anal fissure?
options: Fissure + sentinel skin tag + hypertrophied anal papilla
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.answer: Fissure + sentinel skin tag + hypertrophied anal papilla
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.explanation: A chronic fissure (>6 weeks) develops the triad of fissure + sentinel skin tag + hypertrophied anal papilla. Acute is <6 weeks.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.question: Where are the vast majority of anal fissures located, and why?
options: Anterior midline — the richest blood supply
Anterior and lateral — typical of all fissures
Posterior midline — the poorest blood supply
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.answer: Posterior midline — the poorest blood supply
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.explanation: Most fissures are at the posterior midline (poorest blood supply). Anterior/lateral/multiple fissures suggest a secondary cause (Crohn's, malignancy, infection).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.question: A patient has a fissure that is anterior and lateral with multiple sites. What should this prompt?
options: Reassurance that this is the typical location
Consideration of a secondary cause such as Crohn's, malignancy or infection
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.answer: Consideration of a secondary cause such as Crohn's, malignancy or infection
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.explanation: Anterior/lateral/multiple fissures point away from the typical posterior midline location and should prompt thinking about a secondary cause (Crohn's, malignancy, infection).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.question: How do topical GTN or diltiazem help heal an anal fissure?
options: They contract the sphincter to close the fissure
They numb the area to reduce pain only
They relax the internal sphincter, improving blood flow to allow healing
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.answer: They relax the internal sphincter, improving blood flow to allow healing
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.explanation: Topical GTN or diltiazem relax the internal sphincter, improving blood flow so the fissure can heal.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.question: What is the classic side effect of topical GTN that commonly limits adherence in fissure treatment?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.answer: Headache
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.explanation: GTN's classic side effect is headache, a common reason for poor adherence.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.question: What is the definitive surgical option for a refractory anal fissure, and its notable risk?
options: Lateral internal sphincterotomy — small risk of incontinence
Excision of sinus tracts — risk of bleeding
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.answer: Lateral internal sphincterotomy — small risk of incontinence
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.explanation: For refractory fissures, botulinum toxin injection or lateral internal sphincterotomy (definitive but with a small risk of incontinence) is used.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.question: Approximately what proportion of perianal abscesses arise from cryptoglandular gland infection, and which space is particularly involved?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.answer: ~90%; the intersphincteric space
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.explanation: About 90% of perianal abscesses arise from cryptoglandular gland infection at the dentate line, forming particularly in the intersphincteric space when a gland is blocked. They are twice as common in men.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.question: Which type of perianal abscess is the commonest by location?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.answer: Perianal
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.explanation: By location, perianal is commonest, followed by ischiorectal, intersphincteric and supralevator.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.question: If no abscess is visible and DRE is not possible due to pain/sphincter spasm, what should be suspected?
options: An intersphincteric abscess or anal fissure
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.answer: An intersphincteric abscess or anal fissure
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.explanation: If no abscess is visible and DRE isn't possible because of pain/sphincter spasm, suspect an intersphincteric abscess or anal fissure.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.question: A patient has a clearly visible, tender, fluctuant perianal abscess. What is the appropriate management timeframe?
options: Oral antibiotics for 1 week then review
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.answer: Surgical drainage within 24 hours
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.explanation: A clearly present abscess needs surgical drainage within 24h (no further investigations required first), especially urgent in diabetes, systemic sepsis or immunocompromise. MRI/EUA is for complex/recurrent disease.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.question: Which red-flag complication of a perianal abscess is a surgical emergency?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.answer: Fournier's gangrene (necrotising perineal infection)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.explanation: Fournier's gangrene — a necrotising perineal infection — is the red-flag surgical emergency.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.question: What is a fistula-in-ano?
options: A split in the distal anal mucosa
Enlargement of the anal vascular cushions
A hair-containing sinus in the natal cleft
A localised collection of pus only
A chronic epithelial-lined tract connecting the anorectal lumen to the perineal/buttock skin
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.answer: A chronic epithelial-lined tract connecting the anorectal lumen to the perineal/buttock skin
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.explanation: A fistula-in-ano is a chronic abnormal epithelial-lined tract connecting the anorectal lumen (internal opening) to the perineal/buttock skin (external opening).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.question: What is the approximate risk of a fistula forming after a perianal abscess?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.explanation: A fistula follows chronic cryptoglandular infection; the risk of a fistula after an abscess is approximately 14–38%.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.question: According to Goodsall's rule, how does an anterior external fistula opening track?
options: In a curved path to the posterior midline
It never connects to the anal canal
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.answer: Radially/straight to the anal canal
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.explanation: Goodsall's rule: an anterior external opening tracks radially/straight to the anal canal, whereas a posterior one tracks in a curved path to the posterior midline.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.question: Which investigation is used to map a complex or Crohn's-related fistula tract?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.answer: MRI pelvis
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.explanation: MRI pelvis (with EUA) is used to map the tract, especially for complex or Crohn's-related fistulae.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.question: When is a seton preferred over fistulotomy in fistula-in-ano management?
options: For low, simple tracts that can be laid open
For high tracts crossing significant sphincter, to preserve continence (especially Crohn's-related)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.answer: For high tracts crossing significant sphincter, to preserve continence (especially Crohn's-related)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.explanation: A seton is used for high tracts crossing significant sphincter to preserve continence (especially Crohn's-related fistulae). Fistulotomy lays open low/simple tracts.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.question: What is a pilonidal sinus, and which patient is typically affected?
options: An enlargement of the anal cushions; an elderly woman
A split in the anal mucosa; a constipated child
A tract from the anal lumen to the skin; a Crohn's patient
A pus collection at the dentate line; an immunocompromised patient
A hair-containing sinus in the natal cleft; a young, hirsute male who sits for prolonged periods
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.answer: A hair-containing sinus in the natal cleft; a young, hirsute male who sits for prolonged periods
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.explanation: A pilonidal sinus is a hair-containing sinus tract in the natal cleft (sacrococcygeal); the typical patient is a young, hirsute male with a sedentary/prolonged-sitting lifestyle.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.question: Which examination finding is characteristic of a pilonidal sinus?
options: A sentinel skin tag at the posterior midline
Visible midline pits in the natal cleft
An external opening tracking to the anal canal
A fluctuant lump at the dentate line
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.answer: Visible midline pits in the natal cleft
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.explanation: A pilonidal sinus shows intermittent natal-cleft discharge/swelling and visible midline pits, presenting acutely as a painful pilonidal abscess.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.question: How is an acute pilonidal abscess managed, and what conservative advice is given?
options: Incision + drainage; keep the area clean and shaved
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.answer: Incision + drainage; keep the area clean and shaved
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.explanation: An acute pilonidal abscess is managed with incision + drainage; chronic/recurrent disease needs excision of the sinus tracts with hygiene/hair-removal advice, and conservative advice is to keep the area clean and shaved.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.question: A 40-year-old reports painless bright red bleeding seen on the paper and covering the pan after defecation, with a lump that prolapses on straining but reduces by itself. Proctoscopy shows enlarged cushions. What is the diagnosis and grade?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.answer: 2nd-degree haemorrhoids
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.explanation: Painless bright red surface bleeding with a lump that prolapses on defecation and reduces spontaneously is 2nd-degree haemorrhoids. Blood on the surface (not mixed in) supports a haemorrhoidal rather than cancer source.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.question: A young adult has intense tearing pain on defecation lasting hours, with small-volume bright red blood on the paper, and is too tender for DRE. Examination under anaesthesia shows a posterior midline tear. What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Conservative measures (fibre, fluids, stool softeners, sitz baths) plus topical GTN or diltiazem
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.answer: Conservative measures (fibre, fluids, stool softeners, sitz baths) plus topical GTN or diltiazem
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.explanation: This is a typical posterior midline anal fissure. First-line is conservative (fibre, fluids, stool softeners, topical analgesia, sitz baths) with topical GTN or diltiazem to relax the internal sphincter; surgery is reserved for refractory cases.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.question: A diabetic man presents with a painful, throbbing, tender fluctuant perianal lump, erythema and fever. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Surgical drainage within 24 hours, given the urgency in diabetes
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.answer: Surgical drainage within 24 hours, given the urgency in diabetes
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.explanation: A clearly present perianal abscess needs surgical drainage within 24h, which is especially urgent in diabetes, systemic sepsis or immunocompromise. Watch for Fournier's gangrene as a red flag.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.question: A patient with known Crohn's disease has recurrent perianal abscesses and persistent faeculent discharge from an external opening, with a palpable cord. MRI maps a high tract crossing significant sphincter. What is the most appropriate surgical management?
options: Fistulotomy to lay the tract open
Seton insertion to preserve continence, plus treating the underlying Crohn's
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.answer: Seton insertion to preserve continence, plus treating the underlying Crohn's
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Anorectal/.explanation: A high tract crossing significant sphincter, especially Crohn's-related, is managed with a seton to preserve continence, alongside treating the underlying Crohn's. Fistulotomy is reserved for low/simple tracts.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.question: Which artery supplies the midgut and is the key vessel in acute mesenteric ischaemia?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.explanation: The SMA supplies the midgut (3rd duodenum to splenic flexure) and is the key vessel in acute ischaemia. The coeliac supplies the foregut (rarely ischaemic — rich collaterals) and the IMA supplies the hindgut.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.question: Where is the watershed area between the SMA and IMA territories?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.explanation: The watershed is the splenic flexure (SMA/IMA border). In ischaemic colitis the rectosigmoid junction (IMA/internal iliac) is also a watershed area.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.question: Why is the coeliac artery territory rarely ischaemic?
options: It supplies the hindgut with a single end-artery
It has the highest flow of the three vessels
It supplies the foregut and has rich collaterals
It is never affected by atherosclerosis
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.answer: It supplies the foregut and has rich collaterals
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.explanation: The coeliac artery supplies the foregut and is rarely ischaemic because of rich collaterals.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.question: Which mechanism underlies chronic mesenteric ischaemia?
options: Sudden embolic occlusion of the SMA
A low-flow state with no clot
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.explanation: Chronic mesenteric ischaemia is caused by atherosclerosis gradually narrowing the vessels; acute is sudden occlusion of the SMA.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.question: Which is the key risk factor for acute mesenteric ischaemia of the embolic type?
options: Atrial fibrillation (LA thrombus embolising to the SMA)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.answer: Atrial fibrillation (LA thrombus embolising to the SMA)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.explanation: AF is the key risk factor — a left atrial thrombus embolises to the SMA. Chronic mesenteric ischaemia is associated with a CVD profile (age, smoking, DM, HTN).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.question: A patient describes central colicky abdominal pain about 30 minutes after eating, with weight loss from avoiding food. Which condition is this, and what is the pain called?
options: Acute mesenteric ischaemia — pain out of proportion
Ischaemic colitis — lower-left pain with bloody diarrhoea
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.explanation: Chronic mesenteric ischaemia causes postprandial colicky pain ('intestinal angina') with weight loss from food avoidance, often with an abdominal bruit.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.question: What is the classic triad of chronic mesenteric ischaemia?
options: Postprandial central colicky pain, weight loss and an abdominal bruit
Bloody diarrhoea, fever and raised CRP
Pain out of proportion, lactic acidosis and AF
Rectal bleeding, tenesmus and mucus PR
RIF pain, anaemia and a palpable mass
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.answer: Postprandial central colicky pain, weight loss and an abdominal bruit
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.explanation: The classic triad is postprandial central colicky pain (~30 min after eating), weight loss (food avoidance + malabsorption) and an abdominal bruit.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.question: What classic exam point explains why symptoms of chronic mesenteric ischaemia appear only with advanced disease?
options: Only the SMA needs to be mildly narrowed
Symptoms appear with single-vessel disease in all cases
At least 2 of the 3 vessels must be significantly stenosed before symptoms appear, as collaterals compensate
The coeliac artery must be totally occluded first
There are no collaterals in the mesenteric circulation
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.answer: At least 2 of the 3 vessels must be significantly stenosed before symptoms appear, as collaterals compensate
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.explanation: At least 2 of the 3 vessels must be significantly stenosed before symptoms appear, because collateral supply compensates.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.question: What is the diagnostic test of choice for chronic mesenteric ischaemia?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.explanation: CT angiography is the diagnostic test of choice; routine bloods are often normal, and the CV risk profile should be checked.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.question: What is the first-line revascularisation approach in chronic mesenteric ischaemia?
options: Bypass surgery before any endovascular attempt
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.explanation: Endovascular treatment (percutaneous mesenteric angioplasty + stenting) is first-line; open surgery (endarterectomy/bypass) is used if endovascular fails. CV risk factors are modified, with statin + antiplatelet for secondary prevention.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.question: Which is the commonest subtype of acute mesenteric ischaemia, and its mechanism?
options: Thrombotic — acute-on-chronic atherosclerosis of the SMA
Non-occlusive — a low-flow state with no clot
Embolic — a clot from elsewhere lodges in the SMA
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.answer: Embolic — a clot from elsewhere lodges in the SMA
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.explanation: The embolic subtype is commonest — a clot from elsewhere lodges in the SMA, with clues of AF, recent MI, sudden onset and no prior history.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.question: A patient with a long history of postprandial pain and weight loss now develops sudden severe acute mesenteric ischaemia. Which subtype does the preceding history suggest?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.explanation: The thrombotic subtype is acute-on-chronic atherosclerosis of the SMA, distinguished by a preceding chronic mesenteric ischaemia history.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.question: A critically unwell patient in shock on vasopressors develops bowel ischaemia with no demonstrable clot. Which subtype is this?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.explanation: NOMI is a low-flow state with no physical clot, occurring in shock, sepsis, heart failure or with vasopressors.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.question: A younger patient with a thrombophilia develops acute mesenteric ischaemia of slower onset. Which subtype is most likely?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.explanation: The venous subtype (mesenteric vein thrombosis) is suggested by a younger patient, thrombophilia and a slower onset.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.question: What is the cardinal clinical clue of acute mesenteric ischaemia?
options: Acute pain out of proportion to examination findings
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.answer: Acute pain out of proportion to examination findings
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.explanation: Acute pain out of proportion to examination findings is the cardinal clue, with nausea, vomiting and progression to shock/peritonitis/sepsis. An embolic source (AF, valve disease) should be sought.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.question: Which arterial blood gas finding supports a diagnosis of acute mesenteric ischaemia?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.explanation: ABG shows metabolic acidosis with raised lactate — a marker of ischaemic tissue. CT angiography is definitive.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.question: What is the definitive investigation in acute mesenteric ischaemia?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.explanation: CT angiography is definitive, showing vessel occlusion ± bowel changes. Bloods include FBC, U&E, clotting, amylase and LFT, and ABG shows metabolic acidosis with raised lactate.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.question: What does emergency surgery for acute mesenteric ischaemia involve?
options: Conservative management with bowel rest only
Endovascular stenting alone with no laparotomy
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.explanation: Management is IV resuscitation, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (faecal contamination risk), and emergency surgery to resect necrotic bowel and revascularise (thrombectomy/embolectomy), with a second-look laparotomy at 24–48h to reassess viability.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.question: Why is a second-look laparotomy performed at 24–48h in acute mesenteric ischaemia?
options: To take biopsies for cancer staging
To perform a planned anastomosis reversal
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.explanation: A second-look laparotomy at 24–48h is performed to reassess bowel viability after the initial resection and revascularisation.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.question: What is the approximate mortality of acute mesenteric ischaemia if bowel necrosis occurs?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.explanation: Mortality is high (~60–80%) if bowel necrosis occurs, so early CT and urgent surgery are essential.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.question: Which best describes ischaemic colitis?
options: Sudden SMA occlusion affecting the small bowel, catastrophic
Chronic atherosclerotic narrowing causing intestinal angina
Mesenteric vein thrombosis in a young patient
Acute, transient compromise of blood flow to the large bowel, usually self-limiting
A low-flow state from shock affecting the small bowel
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.answer: Acute, transient compromise of blood flow to the large bowel, usually self-limiting
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.explanation: Ischaemic colitis is an acute, transient compromise of blood flow to the large bowel (not small bowel), usually self-limiting and rarely progressing to necrosis.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.question: A patient presents with lower-left abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea, and CT shows thumbprinting. Which condition is this, and how is it usually managed?
options: Ischaemic colitis — conservative (IV fluids, antibiotics, bowel rest)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.answer: Ischaemic colitis — conservative (IV fluids, antibiotics, bowel rest)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.explanation: Lower-left abdominal pain with bloody diarrhoea and thumbprinting (mucosal oedema) on CT/AXR indicates ischaemic colitis, confirmed on colonoscopy. Management is conservative — IV fluids, antibiotics and bowel rest — with surgery only for gangrene/perforation/stricture.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.question: Which statement correctly contrasts acute mesenteric ischaemia with ischaemic colitis?
options: Acute mesenteric ischaemia = IMA/large bowel/conservative; ischaemic colitis = SMA/small bowel/surgery
Both affect the small bowel and require emergency surgery
Acute mesenteric ischaemia = SMA/small bowel/emergency surgery; ischaemic colitis = IMA-watershed/large bowel/conservative
Both affect the large bowel and are self-limiting
Acute mesenteric ischaemia is self-limiting; ischaemic colitis is catastrophic
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.answer: Acute mesenteric ischaemia = SMA/small bowel/emergency surgery; ischaemic colitis = IMA-watershed/large bowel/conservative
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.explanation: Acute mesenteric ischaemia involves the SMA and small bowel, is catastrophic, and needs emergency surgery; ischaemic colitis involves the IMA/watershed and large bowel and is usually self-limiting and managed conservatively.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.question: A 72-year-old with atrial fibrillation presents with sudden severe central abdominal pain that is far worse than the soft, minimally tender abdomen on examination. ABG shows a metabolic acidosis with a raised lactate. What is the most appropriate next investigation and the likely diagnosis?
options: CT angiography; embolic acute mesenteric ischaemia
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.answer: CT angiography; embolic acute mesenteric ischaemia
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Intestinal.explanation: AF, sudden severe pain out of proportion to examination, and a metabolic acidosis with raised lactate point to embolic acute mesenteric ischaemia (LA thrombus embolising to the SMA). CT angiography is the definitive investigation.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.question: Which statement best describes the underlying mechanism of coeliac disease?
options: Autoimmune sensitivity to gluten causing villous atrophy and malabsorption
Mechanical obstruction of the small bowel
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.answer: Autoimmune sensitivity to gluten causing villous atrophy and malabsorption
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.explanation: Coeliac disease is an autoimmune sensitivity to gluten causing immune-mediated mucosal damage → villous atrophy + malabsorption.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.question: Which fraction of gluten triggers coeliac disease, and in which grains is it found?
options: The gliadin fraction, found in wheat, barley and rye
The casein fraction, found in dairy
The albumin fraction, found in eggs
The gliadin fraction, found only in rice and maize
The lactose fraction, found in milk
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.answer: The gliadin fraction, found in wheat, barley and rye
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.explanation: Gluten (the gliadin fraction) is found in wheat, barley and rye, and is the trigger in coeliac disease.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.question: Which triad of histological changes characterises the mucosal damage of coeliac disease?
options: Villous atrophy + crypt hyperplasia + intraepithelial lymphocytosis
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.answer: Villous atrophy + crypt hyperplasia + intraepithelial lymphocytosis
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.explanation: The T-cell-mediated response (HLA-DQ2/DQ8) produces villous atrophy + crypt hyperplasia + intraepithelial lymphocytosis.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.question: Which HLA haplotype is present in around 95% of coeliac patients?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.answer: HLA-DQ2
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.explanation: There is a strong genetic link: HLA-DQ2 (95%) and HLA-DQ8. Coeliac clusters with T1DM, thyroid disease and Addison's.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.question: Which autoimmune conditions cluster with coeliac disease through shared HLA/autoimmune associations?
options: Type 1 diabetes, thyroid disease and Addison's disease
Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis and IBS
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.answer: Type 1 diabetes, thyroid disease and Addison's disease
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.explanation: Coeliac clusters with T1DM, thyroid disease and Addison's, which all share HLA/autoimmune associations.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.question: What is described as the commonest presenting clue of coeliac disease in adults?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.answer: Unexplained anaemia (iron ± folate ± B12)
