conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.explanation: Unexplained anaemia (iron ± folate ± B12) is the commonest presenting clue of coeliac disease in adults.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.question: A patient presents with an intensely itchy, blistering rash on the elbows, knees and buttocks alongside chronic diarrhoea. Which diagnosis should be suspected?
options: Coeliac disease, with the rash being dermatitis herpetiformis
Eczema unrelated to the gut symptoms
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.answer: Coeliac disease, with the rash being dermatitis herpetiformis
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.explanation: Dermatitis herpetiformis is the pathognomonic skin manifestation — an intensely itchy, blistering rash on extensor surfaces (elbows, knees, buttocks). A 'rash + diarrhoea' stem = coeliac until proven otherwise.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.question: An adult has iron-deficiency anaemia that is not responding to iron supplementation, plus chronic fatigue. What is the appropriate next step?
options: Reassure and continue the same iron dose
Start a gluten-free diet before any testing
Test coeliac serology, keeping a low threshold
Repeat the FBC in 6 months with no other action
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.answer: Test coeliac serology, keeping a low threshold
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.explanation: Adults often present subtly or atypically — e.g. 'iron-deficiency anaemia not responding to iron' or chronic fatigue. There should be a low threshold to test serology.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.question: What is the first-line serology test for coeliac disease, and what must always be requested with it?
options: IgE to gluten, with total IgE alongside
HLA-DQ2/DQ8 typing as the first-line test
IgA tissue transglutaminase (IgA tTG), with total IgA alongside
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.answer: IgA tissue transglutaminase (IgA tTG), with total IgA alongside
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.explanation: IgA tTG is the first-line serology test, and total IgA must always be requested alongside it because of the IgA deficiency trap.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.question: What is the gold-standard test for confirming coeliac disease, and what confirms the diagnosis?
options: HLA typing alone confirms the diagnosis
Duodenal biopsy at OGD; positive serology + positive biopsy confirms the diagnosis
A single positive IgA tTG confirms the diagnosis without biopsy in all adults
Blood film showing Howell-Jolly bodies confirms the diagnosis
Resolution of symptoms on a gluten-free diet confirms the diagnosis
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.answer: Duodenal biopsy at OGD; positive serology + positive biopsy confirms the diagnosis
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.explanation: Duodenal biopsy at OGD is the gold standard (villous atrophy + crypt hyperplasia + intraepithelial lymphocytosis + lamina propria lymphocytic infiltrate). Positive serology + positive biopsy = confirmed diagnosis.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.question: A patient started a gluten-free diet two weeks ago and now has negative coeliac serology and normal-looking villi on biopsy. Why might this be a false negative?
options: Serology is always unreliable in adults
IgA deficiency is the only cause of false negatives
Biopsy is never affected by diet
A gluten-free diet normalises antibodies and heals villi; the patient must eat gluten for ≥6 weeks before testing
The test should have been IgE-based
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.answer: A gluten-free diet normalises antibodies and heals villi; the patient must eat gluten for ≥6 weeks before testing
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.explanation: Testing trap 1: the patient must be on a gluten-containing diet for ≥6 weeks (gluten in ≥1 meal/day) before serology and biopsy. A gluten-free diet normalises antibodies and heals villi → a false-negative result.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.question: A patient with strong clinical features of coeliac disease has a negative IgA tTG, but their total IgA is low. What is the appropriate action?
options: Repeat the IgA tTG after starting a gluten-free diet
Request HLA typing as the definitive test
Start lifelong gluten-free diet without further testing
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.answer: Use IgG-based tests (IgG-DGP or IgG-tTG)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.explanation: Testing trap 2: coeliac is associated with selective IgA deficiency. If IgA is low, IgA-tTG is falsely negative despite active disease — check total IgA and, if deficient, use IgG-based tests (IgG-DGP or IgG-tTG).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.question: What is the only curative treatment for coeliac disease, and how is adherence monitored?
options: Pancreatic enzyme replacement, monitored with faecal elastase
A lifelong gluten-free diet, monitored with serial tTG
Iron supplementation alone, monitored with ferritin
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.answer: A lifelong gluten-free diet, monitored with serial tTG
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.explanation: A lifelong gluten-free diet is the only curative treatment (avoid wheat, barley, rye; oats usually tolerated unless contaminated). Villi recover and serology normalises; adherence is monitored with serial tTG.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.question: Why is pneumococcal vaccination recommended in coeliac disease?
options: Gluten directly suppresses the immune system
Functional hyposplenism increases susceptibility to encapsulated bacteria
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.answer: Functional hyposplenism increases susceptibility to encapsulated bacteria
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.explanation: Functional hyposplenism increases susceptibility to encapsulated bacteria (Pneumococcus, Hib, Meningococcus), so patients are vaccinated with a 5-yearly booster — the same logic as sickle cell/other asplenic states.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.question: When is osteoporosis screening with DEXA indicated in coeliac disease?
options: In every newly diagnosed patient regardless of duration
If there is prolonged untreated disease
Never, as bone density is unaffected
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.answer: If there is prolonged untreated disease
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.explanation: Deficiencies (iron, folate, B12, calcium, vitamin D) are replaced as indicated, and osteoporosis screening (DEXA) is performed if there is prolonged untreated disease.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.question: Which anaemia pattern combination is correct for the malabsorption anaemias of coeliac disease?
options: All malabsorption anaemias produce a normal MCV
Iron deficiency ↓MCV; folate and B12 deficiency ↑MCV (B12 also neurological)
Folate deficiency causes only neurological signs
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.answer: Iron deficiency ↓MCV; folate and B12 deficiency ↑MCV (B12 also neurological)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.explanation: The malabsorption anaemias are iron deficiency (↓MCV), folate deficiency (↑MCV) and B12 deficiency (↑MCV + neurological), often a mixed picture.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.question: Why do osteoporosis and osteomalacia occur in coeliac disease?
options: Calcium and vitamin D malabsorption reduces bone density
Excess vitamin D absorption raises calcium
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.answer: Calcium and vitamin D malabsorption reduces bone density
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.explanation: Calcium and vitamin D malabsorption reduces bone density, increasing fracture risk, and is monitored with DEXA.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.question: A blood film in coeliac disease shows Howell-Jolly bodies. What does this indicate, and why does it matter?
options: Functional hyposplenism, which raises infection risk from encapsulated organisms and drives vaccination
Vitamin B12 deficiency with neurological signs
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.answer: Functional hyposplenism, which raises infection risk from encapsulated organisms and drives vaccination
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.explanation: Howell-Jolly bodies (nuclear remnants normally culled by the spleen) indicate functional hyposplenism, raising infection risk from encapsulated organisms and driving vaccination.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.question: What is the key malignancy associated with coeliac disease?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.answer: Enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma (EATL)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.explanation: EATL (enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma) is the key malignancy of coeliac disease. Coeliac is also associated with small-bowel adenocarcinoma and oesophageal cancer.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.question: A patient with well-controlled coeliac disease on a strict gluten-free diet develops new B-symptoms and weight loss. What should be suspected?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.answer: Enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma (EATL)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.explanation: New B-symptoms or weight loss despite a strict gluten-free diet should raise suspicion of EATL, the key malignancy of coeliac disease.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.question: A 30-year-old with chronic diarrhoea (pale, floating stools), bloating and unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia is being investigated for coeliac disease. They mention they have already been gluten-free for a month and feel better. What is the most appropriate next step before serology?
options: Proceed straight to serology while gluten-free
Diagnose coeliac on symptom response alone
Request HLA-DQ2/DQ8 typing as the confirmatory test
Advise reintroducing gluten for ≥6 weeks before serology and biopsy
Start lifelong gluten-free diet and arrange DEXA
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.answer: Advise reintroducing gluten for ≥6 weeks before serology and biopsy
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.explanation: Testing requires a gluten-containing diet for ≥6 weeks (gluten in ≥1 meal/day) because a gluten-free diet normalises antibodies and heals villi, causing false negatives. The patient should reintroduce gluten before serology and biopsy.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.question: A newly diagnosed coeliac patient (positive IgA tTG and confirmatory biopsy) asks about treatment and ongoing care. Which single plan is most consistent with the notes?
options: Lifelong gluten-free diet, pneumococcal vaccination, deficiency replacement, and serial tTG monitoring
Gluten-free diet only, with no vaccination or monitoring
Iron supplementation alone with no dietary change
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.answer: Lifelong gluten-free diet, pneumococcal vaccination, deficiency replacement, and serial tTG monitoring
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Coeliac Di.explanation: Management is a lifelong gluten-free diet (the only curative treatment), pneumococcal vaccination (for functional hyposplenism), replacement of deficiencies (iron, folate, B12, calcium, vitamin D), and adherence monitoring with serial tTG.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: Which statement about the control of GI motility is correct?
options: The CNS generates the basic motility patterns; the gut cannot function without it
Sympathetic activity increases motility ('rest and digest')
Interstitial cells of Cajal inhibit contraction
The enteric nervous system runs motility semi-autonomously (more neurons than the spinal cord); the brain modulates but doesn't generate the basic patterns
Gut hormones have no role in motility
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: The enteric nervous system runs motility semi-autonomously (more neurons than the spinal cord); the brain modulates but doesn't generate the basic patterns
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: The enteric nervous system runs motility semi-autonomously (it has more neurons than the spinal cord); the brain modulates but doesn't generate the basic patterns. Parasympathetic (vagus) increases motility; interstitial cells of Cajal are the pacemakers generating slow waves.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: Which correctly matches an enteric plexus to its function?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: Myenteric (Auerbach's) → motility; submucosal (Meissner's) → secretion/blood flow
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: The myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus controls motility; the submucosal (Meissner's) plexus controls secretion/blood flow. Slow waves are generated by the interstitial cells of Cajal.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: How do peristalsis and segmentation differ?
options: Peristalsis is propulsion (a coordinated wave moving contents forward); segmentation is mixing (localised contractions, no net forward movement)
Segmentation occurs mainly in the oesophagus
Peristalsis occurs only in the small intestine
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: Peristalsis is propulsion (a coordinated wave moving contents forward); segmentation is mixing (localised contractions, no net forward movement)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: Peristalsis is propulsion — a coordinated wave (contraction behind, relaxation ahead) that moves contents forward. Segmentation is mixing — localised contractions that churn contents with no net forward movement (mainly small intestine). 'Peristalsis moves, segmentation mixes.'

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: A patient presents with dysphagia. Manometry shows a lower oesophageal sphincter that fails to relax and absent oesophageal peristalsis. What is the diagnosis and mechanism?
options: Achalasia — LOS fails to relax + absent peristalsis (loss of myenteric plexus neurons)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: Achalasia — LOS fails to relax + absent peristalsis (loss of myenteric plexus neurons)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: Achalasia = LOS fails to relax + absent oesophageal peristalsis → dysphagia, due to loss of myenteric plexus neurons. GORD is the opposite — a lax/incompetent LOS causing acid reflux.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: A diabetic patient has nausea, bloating and early satiety, with delayed gastric emptying on studies. What is the diagnosis, and how is it treated?
options: Gastroparesis (diabetic autonomic neuropathy); treat with prokinetics
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: Gastroparesis (diabetic autonomic neuropathy); treat with prokinetics
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: Gastroparesis is delayed gastric emptying (often from diabetic autonomic neuropathy) causing nausea/bloating; it is treated with prokinetics.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: What is the Migrating Motor Complex (MMC), and which drug mimics its trigger?
options: A post-meal mixing wave; mimicked by loperamide
The gastrocolic reflex; mimicked by metoclopramide
The defecation reflex; mimicked by domperidone
A periodic between-meal 'housekeeping' peristaltic wave that sweeps residual contents (stimulated by motilin); erythromycin mimics motilin → prokinetic
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: A periodic between-meal 'housekeeping' peristaltic wave that sweeps residual contents (stimulated by motilin); erythromycin mimics motilin → prokinetic
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: The MMC is a periodic between-meal 'housekeeping' peristaltic wave that sweeps residual contents through, stimulated by motilin. Erythromycin mimics motilin, acting as a prokinetic.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: A neonate presents with constipation and obstruction. Biopsy shows an aganglionic segment. What is the diagnosis and mechanism?
options: Hirschsprung's disease — absent enteric ganglia → failure of peristalsis → neonatal obstruction/constipation
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: Hirschsprung's disease — absent enteric ganglia → failure of peristalsis → neonatal obstruction/constipation
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: Hirschsprung's disease is an aganglionic segment (absent enteric ganglia) → failure of peristalsis → neonatal obstruction/constipation.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: In which situation should the anti-motility drug loperamide be avoided?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: Inflammatory or bloody (infective) diarrhoea
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: Loperamide reduces gut motility for diarrhoea but should be avoided in inflammatory or bloody (infective) diarrhoea.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: Parietal cells secrete acid via the H⁺/K⁺ ATPase. Which three signals converge to stimulate this, and which drug blocks the final common step?
options: Secretin, CCK, motilin; blocked by H2 blockers
Somatostatin, gastrin, secretin; blocked by loperamide
Histamine, secretin, prostaglandins; blocked by NSAIDs
ACh, secretin, motilin; blocked by octreotide
Gastrin, histamine (via H2 receptors), and ACh (vagus); the proton pump is blocked by PPIs (the most powerful)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: Gastrin, histamine (via H2 receptors), and ACh (vagus); the proton pump is blocked by PPIs (the most powerful)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: Acid secretion is stimulated by three converging signals: gastrin (G cells), histamine (ECL cells, via H2 receptors) and ACh (vagus). PPIs block the proton pump (final common step — most powerful); H2 blockers block histamine's contribution.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: A patient develops macrocytic anaemia after total gastrectomy. What is the mechanism?
options: Loss of pancreatic enzymes → B12 malabsorption
Loss of parietal cells → loss of intrinsic factor → B12 malabsorption in the terminal ileum
Loss of bile salts → B12 malabsorption
Loss of chief cells → pepsin deficiency
Loss of G cells → gastrin deficiency
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: Loss of parietal cells → loss of intrinsic factor → B12 malabsorption in the terminal ileum
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: Parietal cells make intrinsic factor, essential for B12 absorption in the terminal ileum. Their loss (gastrectomy, or autoimmune destruction in pernicious anaemia) causes B12 deficiency and macrocytic anaemia.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: Why does chronic NSAID use predispose to peptic ulcers?
options: NSAIDs stimulate the proton pump directly
NSAIDs block prostaglandins, which (with the mucus-bicarbonate barrier) protect the stomach from its own acid
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: NSAIDs block prostaglandins, which (with the mucus-bicarbonate barrier) protect the stomach from its own acid
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: The stomach is protected by the mucus-bicarbonate barrier + prostaglandins. NSAIDs block prostaglandins, weakening this defence → peptic ulcers (as does H. pylori).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: How does the pancreas avoid digesting itself, and what happens when this fails?
options: Proteases are secreted as inactive zymogens (e.g. trypsinogen) activated only in the duodenum; premature intra-pancreatic activation → autodigestion → acute pancreatitis
It secretes only bicarbonate; failure causes gastritis
Enzymes are secreted fully active but neutralised by acid
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: Proteases are secreted as inactive zymogens (e.g. trypsinogen) activated only in the duodenum; premature intra-pancreatic activation → autodigestion → acute pancreatitis
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: Pancreatic proteases are secreted as inactive zymogens (e.g. trypsinogen) and activated only in the duodenum (enterokinase → trypsin → activates the rest). Premature intra-pancreatic activation → the pancreas autodigests → acute pancreatitis.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: A patient with cystic fibrosis has steatorrhoea and weight loss from pancreatic exocrine insufficiency. What is the treatment principle?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: Pancreatic enzyme replacement (Creon)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency (chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis) → ↓enzymes → malabsorption + steatorrhoea, treated with enzyme replacement (Creon).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: Which describes the three phases of digestion correctly?
options: Cephalic (food in stomach); gastric (sight/smell); intestinal (chyme in duodenum)
Cephalic (chyme in duodenum); gastric (vagal); intestinal (food in stomach)
All three phases are triggered by acid in the duodenum
Only the gastric phase involves any secretion
Cephalic (sight/smell/thought, vagal); gastric (food in stomach → gastrin → acid); intestinal (chyme in duodenum → CCK + secretin)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: Cephalic (sight/smell/thought, vagal); gastric (food in stomach → gastrin → acid); intestinal (chyme in duodenum → CCK + secretin)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: Cephalic phase: sight/smell/taste/thought of food (vagal) → anticipatory secretion. Gastric phase: food in the stomach → gastrin → acid; peak secretion. Intestinal phase: chyme entering the duodenum → CCK + secretin regulate pancreas/bile and feedback-inhibit the stomach.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: A patient repeatedly vomiting gastric contents develops an acid-base disturbance. Which is it and why?
options: Metabolic alkalosis from loss of gastric H⁺
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: Metabolic alkalosis from loss of gastric H⁺
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: Vomiting causes loss of gastric H⁺ → metabolic alkalosis.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: How is the small intestinal surface area amplified for absorption, and what disease reduces it?
options: Circular folds → villi → microvilli (brush border); reduced by coeliac disease (villous atrophy)
The brush border has no digestive role
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: Circular folds → villi → microvilli (brush border); reduced by coeliac disease (villous atrophy)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: Surface area is amplified by circular folds → villi → microvilli (brush border), which also carries the final digestive enzymes. Coeliac disease causes villous atrophy → loss of surface area → malabsorption.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: Which transporters absorb the monosaccharides, and why does lactase deficiency cause symptoms?
options: Glucose/galactose via SGLT1 (Na⁺-coupled), fructose via GLUT5, exit via GLUT2; lactase deficiency → undigested lactose → osmotic diarrhoea + fermentation
Fructose via SGLT1; lactase deficiency causes constipation
All monosaccharides via GLUT2 only; lactase deficiency raises blood glucose
Glucose via GLUT5; lactase deficiency is asymptomatic
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: Glucose/galactose via SGLT1 (Na⁺-coupled), fructose via GLUT5, exit via GLUT2; lactase deficiency → undigested lactose → osmotic diarrhoea + fermentation
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: Only monosaccharides are absorbed: glucose + galactose via SGLT1 (Na⁺-coupled, active), fructose via GLUT5 (facilitated), then GLUT2 out into blood. Lactase deficiency → undigested lactose → osmotic diarrhoea + bacterial fermentation (bloating, wind).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: Which statement about fat absorption and its transport route is correct?
options: Fats are absorbed as chylomicrons directly into the portal blood
Fat needs no bile for absorption

Fatty acids/monoglycerides are re-esterified into triglycerides, packaged into chylomicrons that enter the lymphatics (lacteals) → thoracic duct → blood, unlike carbs/proteins which go into the portal blood
Fat is absorbed in the terminal ileum only
Chylomicrons are small enough to enter capillaries directly
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: Fatty acids/monoglycerides are re-esterified into triglycerides, packaged into chylomicrons that enter the lymphatics (lacteals) → thoracic duct → blood, unlike carbs/proteins which go into the portal blood
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: After digestion, fatty acids/monoglycerides diffuse into the enterocyte → re-esterified into triglycerides → packaged into chylomicrons. These are too big for capillaries, so they enter the lymphatics (lacteals) → thoracic duct → blood, whereas carbs/proteins go straight into the portal blood.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: Steatorrhoea is the common endpoint of fat maldigestion/malabsorption. Which trio of mechanisms produces it?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: ↓bile (can't emulsify), ↓lipase (can't digest), ↓surface (can't absorb)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: Steatorrhoea results from ↓bile (obstruction, cholestasis, bile-salt malabsorption → can't emulsify), ↓lipase (pancreatic insufficiency, CF → can't digest), or ↓surface (coeliac, Crohn's → can't absorb).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: A patient with Crohn's disease affecting the terminal ileum (or after ileal resection) is at risk of which two specific problems?
options: B12 deficiency + bile-salt malabsorption (with diarrhoea and fat malabsorption)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: B12 deficiency + bile-salt malabsorption (with diarrhoea and fat malabsorption)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: B12 (needs intrinsic factor) and bile salts (recycled via enterohepatic circulation) are absorbed in the terminal ileum, so Crohn's/ileal resection causes B12 deficiency + bile-salt malabsorption (→ diarrhoea + fat malabsorption).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: Where is iron principally absorbed, and what condition affecting that site causes iron deficiency?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: Duodenum (+ proximal jejunum); coeliac/duodenal disease
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: Iron is absorbed in the duodenum (+ proximal jejunum), so coeliac/duodenal disease can cause iron deficiency.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: In coeliac disease, what is the sequence linking gluten to malabsorption?
options: Gluten → villous atrophy → ↓surface area → malabsorption (iron, folate, fat → steatorrhoea, weight loss)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: Gluten → villous atrophy → ↓surface area → malabsorption (iron, folate, fat → steatorrhoea, weight loss)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: In coeliac disease, gluten → villous atrophy → ↓surface area → malabsorption of iron, folate and fat, producing steatorrhoea and weight loss.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: Which gut hormone-cell-stimulus-action set is CORRECT?
options: Secretin — G cells — fat — gallbladder contraction
CCK — I cells (duodenum/jejunum) — fat + protein — gallbladder contraction + pancreatic enzymes + satiety; slows gastric emptying
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: CCK — I cells (duodenum/jejunum) — fat + protein — gallbladder contraction + pancreatic enzymes + satiety; slows gastric emptying
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: CCK is from I cells (duodenum/jejunum), stimulated by fat + protein, causing gallbladder contraction + pancreatic enzyme secretion + satiety, and slowing gastric emptying. Gastrin is from G cells (→ acid); secretin is from S cells (→ bicarbonate to acid).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: State the pairing logic of CCK and secretin in the duodenum.
options: CCK responds to acid; secretin to fat
CCK responds to fat/protein (brings bile + enzymes to digest); secretin responds to acid (brings bicarbonate to neutralise) — the stimulus predicts the response
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: CCK responds to fat/protein (brings bile + enzymes to digest); secretin responds to acid (brings bicarbonate to neutralise) — the stimulus predicts the response
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: CCK responds to fat + protein → gallbladder contraction (bile to emulsify fat) + pancreatic enzymes (to digest). Secretin responds to acid → bicarbonate (to neutralise). The stimulus always predicts the response.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: A patient has multiple, refractory peptic ulcers (including atypical sites) with diarrhoea despite PPI therapy. Which diagnosis and mechanism fit?
options: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome — a gastrinoma → unregulated acid → multiple/refractory ulcers
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome — a gastrinoma → unregulated acid → multiple/refractory ulcers
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is a gastrinoma (gastrin-secreting tumour, often pancreatic/duodenal) → unregulated acid → multiple/refractory peptic ulcers (including atypical sites) with diarrhoea — think of it with recurrent ulcers despite PPI.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: What is the incretin effect, and which hormones mediate it?
options: IV glucose triggers more insulin than oral glucose; mediated by gastrin
It is the suppression of insulin by CCK
It is mediated by secretin and motilin
Oral glucose triggers more insulin than the same glucose given IV, because the gut releases GIP + GLP-1 which prime the pancreas before glucose hits the blood
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: Oral glucose triggers more insulin than the same glucose given IV, because the gut releases GIP + GLP-1 which prime the pancreas before glucose hits the blood
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: The incretin effect: oral glucose triggers more insulin than the same glucose given IV, because the gut releases GIP + GLP-1, which prime the pancreas before glucose even hits the blood (feed-forward). Both are broken down by DPP-4.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: How do GLP-1 agonists and DPP-4 inhibitors work in type 2 diabetes, and why is hypoglycaemia risk low?
options: GLP-1 agonists (resist DPP-4) → ↑insulin, satiety, weight loss; DPP-4 inhibitors block incretin breakdown → ↑endogenous incretins; their action is glucose-dependent, so hypo risk is low
GLP-1 agonists block insulin; DPP-4 inhibitors raise glucagon
Both directly stimulate the proton pump
Both slow gastric emptying by blocking motilin
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: GLP-1 agonists (resist DPP-4) → ↑insulin, satiety, weight loss; DPP-4 inhibitors block incretin breakdown → ↑endogenous incretins; their action is glucose-dependent, so hypo risk is low
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: GLP-1 agonists (semaglutide, liraglutide — resist DPP-4) increase insulin, satiety and weight loss; DPP-4 inhibitors ('gliptins') block incretin breakdown → more endogenous incretins. Their glucose-dependent action gives a low hypoglycaemia risk.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: Which hormone is the 'hunger hormone', where is it made, and how does it behave around meals?
options: Leptin, from adipose tissue, rises after meals
PYY, from L cells, drives hunger
Ghrelin, from the stomach (fundus), rises before meals and falls after eating
CCK, from I cells, drives hunger
Somatostatin, from D cells, drives hunger
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: Ghrelin, from the stomach (fundus), rises before meals and falls after eating
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: Ghrelin is the 'hunger hormone', made in the stomach fundus; it rises before meals (driving appetite) and falls after eating.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: Somatostatin is a universal inhibitor of GI secretions. Which drug is its analogue, and what is it used for?
options: Octreotide; used for variceal bleeds, acromegaly, neuroendocrine tumours/carcinoid
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: Octreotide; used for variceal bleeds, acromegaly, neuroendocrine tumours/carcinoid
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: Somatostatin (D cells) is a universal inhibitor of acid, gut hormones and pancreatic/GI secretions. Its analogue octreotide is used for variceal bleeds, acromegaly and neuroendocrine tumours/carcinoid.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: A patient with a neuroendocrine tumour has episodic flushing and diarrhoea from vasoactive substance (serotonin) secretion. What is the syndrome and its treatment?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: Carcinoid syndrome; treated with octreotide
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: Carcinoid syndrome is a neuroendocrine tumour secreting vasoactive substances (serotonin) → flushing and diarrhoea, treated with octreotide (a somatostatin analogue).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: Which satiety and hunger signals converge on the hypothalamus, and which is the long-term energy-store signal?
options: Ghrelin drives satiety; CCK drives hunger
Leptin drives hunger; ghrelin drives long-term satiety
Ghrelin drives hunger (empty stomach); CCK, GLP-1 and PYY give meal-to-meal satiety; leptin (from fat stores) signals long-term energy balance
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: Ghrelin drives hunger (empty stomach); CCK, GLP-1 and PYY give meal-to-meal satiety; leptin (from fat stores) signals long-term energy balance
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: Ghrelin (from the empty stomach) drives hunger; CCK, GLP-1 and PYY give short-term (meal-to-meal) satiety; leptin (from fat stores) signals long-term energy balance. All converge on the hypothalamus (arcuate nucleus).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: Why is the liver the first organ to process everything absorbed from the gut, and what is the clinical consequence?
options: It receives ~70% of its blood from the portal vein (nutrient-rich, straight from the gut) plus ~30% from the hepatic artery → first-pass metabolism, which lowers the oral bioavailability of some drugs
It receives only hepatic arterial blood; this raises oral bioavailability
The gut drains directly into the systemic circulation, bypassing the liver
Kupffer cells absorb all drugs first
The liver has no arterial supply
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: It receives ~70% of its blood from the portal vein (nutrient-rich, straight from the gut) plus ~30% from the hepatic artery → first-pass metabolism, which lowers the oral bioavailability of some drugs
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: The liver has a dual blood supply: portal vein (~70%, nutrient-rich from the gut) + hepatic artery (~30%, oxygenated). Orally-absorbed drugs hit the liver first → first-pass metabolism → low oral bioavailability for some drugs.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: Which are the five core functions of the liver, as a framework for understanding liver disease?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: Metabolism, synthesis, storage, detoxification, excretion
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: The five core liver functions are metabolism, synthesis, storage, detoxification and excretion. Liver disease is understood as the loss of these, making LFTs, bleeding, jaundice and encephalopathy derivable.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: Why does liver failure cause hypoglycaemia?
options: Impaired gluconeogenesis (and glycogen handling) in the failing liver, which normally maintains blood glucose
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: Impaired gluconeogenesis (and glycogen handling) in the failing liver, which normally maintains blood glucose
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: The liver is central to glucose homeostasis (glycogen storage in the fed state; glycogenolysis + gluconeogenesis in the fasted state). Liver failure disrupts this → hypoglycaemia from reduced gluconeogenesis/glycogen.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: A patient with liver failure develops oedema and ascites. Which synthetic deficiency explains this?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: ↓albumin → ↓oncotic pressure → fluid shifts into tissues/peritoneum
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: Albumin is the main plasma protein maintaining oncotic pressure. Liver failure → ↓albumin → ↓oncotic pressure → oedema/ascites.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: Why is PT/INR considered the best marker of synthetic liver function, and why does it rise early?
options: Because albumin has a shorter half-life than clotting factors
Because PT/INR measures hepatocyte damage directly
Because clotting factors are not made in the liver
The liver makes almost all clotting factors, so their loss prolongs PT/INR; it rises early because factor VII has a short half-life
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: The liver makes almost all clotting factors, so their loss prolongs PT/INR; it rises early because factor VII has a short half-life
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: The liver makes almost all clotting factors (including vitamin-K-dependent II, VII, IX, X). Their loss prolongs PT/INR — the best marker of synthetic function, rising early because factor VII has a short half-life. Albumin (long half-life) reflects chronic synthetic function.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: A patient with decompensated liver disease becomes confused with asterixis. What is the mechanism and treatment?
options: ↓ammonia clearance → ↑ammonia (neurotoxic) → hepatic encephalopathy; treat with lactulose (traps ammonia in the gut) + rifaximin (↓ammonia-producing gut bacteria)
↑bilirubin crossing the BBB; treat with phototherapy
↓clotting factors → intracranial bleed; treat with vitamin K
Hypoglycaemia alone; treat with glucose only
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: ↓ammonia clearance → ↑ammonia (neurotoxic) → hepatic encephalopathy; treat with lactulose (traps ammonia in the gut) + rifaximin (↓ammonia-producing gut bacteria)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: The liver converts neurotoxic ammonia to urea. In liver failure, ↓ammonia clearance → ↑ammonia → hepatic encephalopathy (confusion, asterixis, coma), treated with lactulose (traps ammonia in the gut) and rifaximin (reduces ammonia-producing gut bacteria).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: Why do patients with chronic liver disease develop spider naevi and gynaecomastia?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: ↓oestrogen clearance by the failing liver
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: The liver clears hormones including oestrogen. In liver failure, reduced oestrogen clearance → gynaecomastia and spider naevi.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: On LFTs, a markedly raised ALT and AST with only mild ALP elevation indicates which pattern?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: Hepatocellular (hepatocyte damage, e.g. hepatitis)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: ALT + AST (transaminases) reflect hepatocyte damage, raised ↑↑ in hepatocellular injury (hepatitis). ALP + GGT reflect cholestasis/obstruction. The pattern (ALT/AST vs ALP/GGT) identifies the type of liver problem; transaminases indicate damage, not function.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: A patient has a raised ALP and GGT with relatively normal transaminases. What does the raised GGT tell you, and what pattern is this?
options: GGT confirms bone origin of ALP; hepatocellular pattern
GGT confirms the ALP is hepatic; a cholestatic/obstructive pattern
GGT indicates synthetic failure; pre-hepatic pattern
GGT reflects hepatocyte damage; hepatocellular pattern
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: GGT confirms the ALP is hepatic; a cholestatic/obstructive pattern
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: ALP + GGT are raised in cholestasis/obstruction, and GGT confirms that the ALP rise is hepatic (rather than, e.g., bony). This is the cholestatic pattern.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: Which enzyme conjugates bilirubin in the liver, and what does conjugation achieve?
options: Biliverdin reductase; binds bilirubin to albumin
UDP-glucuronyl transferase; makes bilirubin water-soluble (so it can be excreted in bile and appear in urine)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: UDP-glucuronyl transferase; makes bilirubin water-soluble (so it can be excreted in bile and appear in urine)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: The liver enzyme UDP-glucuronyl transferase conjugates unconjugated (water-insoluble, albumin-bound) bilirubin → conjugated (water-soluble) bilirubin, which can be excreted into bile and can appear in urine.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: Why can conjugated but not unconjugated bilirubin appear in the urine?
options: Conjugation makes bilirubin water-soluble so it can be filtered; unconjugated bilirubin is albumin-bound and can't be filtered
Conjugated is albumin-bound and filtered; unconjugated is free
Both are equally excreted in urine
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: Conjugation makes bilirubin water-soluble so it can be filtered; unconjugated bilirubin is albumin-bound and can't be filtered
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: Conjugation makes bilirubin water-soluble, so conjugated bilirubin can be filtered and appear in urine (dark urine). Unconjugated bilirubin is water-insoluble and albumin-bound, so it can't be filtered — the basis of distinguishing jaundice types.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: Which type of bilirubin crosses the blood-brain barrier, and what is the clinical risk?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: Unconjugated (lipid-soluble); kernicterus risk in neonates
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: Unconjugated bilirubin is lipid-soluble and crosses the BBB, giving a kernicterus risk in neonates. Conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and does not cross.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: A patient with haemolysis has jaundice. What bilirubin picture and urine/stool findings are expected (pre-hepatic pattern)?
options: Unconjugated ↑, normal urine and stool, with ↑LDH, ↓haptoglobin, ↑reticulocytes
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: Unconjugated ↑, normal urine and stool, with ↑LDH, ↓haptoglobin, ↑reticulocytes
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: Pre-hepatic jaundice (haemolysis) raises unconjugated bilirubin, which can't be excreted in urine and has intact downstream conjugation/excretion → normal urine and stool, plus haemolysis labs (↑LDH, ↓haptoglobin, ↑reticulocytes).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: A patient with a common bile duct gallstone has jaundice with dark urine, pale stools and itch. What bilirubin picture and enzyme pattern fit?
options: Conjugated ↑ (can't be excreted → dark urine; no bilirubin reaching gut → pale stools; bile salts → itch), with ↑ALP/GGT
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: Conjugated ↑ (can't be excreted → dark urine; no bilirubin reaching gut → pale stools; bile salts → itch), with ↑ALP/GGT
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: Post-hepatic (obstructive) jaundice raises conjugated bilirubin → dark urine (soluble bilirubin filtered) + pale stools (no bilirubin reaching gut → no stercobilin) + itch (bile salts) + ↑ALP/GGT (cholestatic).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: A well young adult develops mild jaundice only during fasting or intercurrent illness, with isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and otherwise normal LFTs. What is the diagnosis and management?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: Gilbert's syndrome (benign mild ↓conjugation); reassurance only
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: Gilbert's syndrome is a benign mild reduction in conjugation (mild ↓UDP-glucuronyl transferase) → mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, often noticed during illness/fasting/stress. Management is reassurance only.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: A neonate develops unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. Why, and how is severe cases treated?
options: Immature liver conjugation + high red cell turnover → unconjugated bilirubin (kernicterus risk as it crosses the immature BBB); treat with phototherapy (converts bilirubin to a water-soluble form)
Mature conjugation with low red cell turnover; treat with exchange transfusion only
Biliary obstruction → conjugated bilirubin; treat with surgery
Gilbert's syndrome; no treatment ever needed
Excess albumin binding; treat with albumin infusion
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: Immature liver conjugation + high red cell turnover → unconjugated bilirubin (kernicterus risk as it crosses the immature BBB); treat with phototherapy (converts bilirubin to a water-soluble form)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: Neonatal jaundice arises from immature liver conjugation + high red cell turnover → unconjugated bilirubin, which crosses the immature BBB (kernicterus risk). Phototherapy converts bilirubin to a water-soluble form.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: Using urine and stool findings alone, how are the jaundice types distinguished?
options: Dark urine = pre-hepatic; pale stool = pre-hepatic
Pale urine = obstruction; dark stool = pre-hepatic
Dark urine = conjugated; pale stool = obstruction; normal both = pre-hepatic
Normal urine with pale stool = hepatocellular
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: Dark urine = conjugated; pale stool = obstruction; normal both = pre-hepatic
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: Dark urine = conjugated bilirubinaemia; pale stool = obstruction (no bilirubin reaching the gut); normal urine and stool = pre-hepatic (haemolysis).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: What are the two jobs of bile, and what does disrupting its flow or composition cause?
options: Protein digestion and acid neutralisation; disruption causes ulcers
Carbohydrate digestion and vitamin storage; disruption causes diabetes
Sterilisation and B12 absorption; disruption causes pernicious anaemia
Only fat digestion; disruption causes nothing significant
Fat digestion (bile salts) and excretion (bilirubin, cholesterol, drugs); disruption causes gallstones, fat malabsorption and cholestasis
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: Fat digestion (bile salts) and excretion (bilirubin, cholesterol, drugs); disruption causes gallstones, fat malabsorption and cholestasis
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: Bile has two jobs: fat digestion (bile salts) and excretion (bilirubin, cholesterol, drugs). Disrupting bile flow or composition causes gallstones, fat malabsorption and cholestasis.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: What keeps cholesterol soluble in bile, and what tips the balance toward gallstones?
options: Bilirubin keeps it soluble; excess bicarbonate causes stones
Bile salts + phospholipids (lecithin) keep cholesterol dissolved; excess cholesterol (or ↓bile salts) → cholesterol precipitates → gallstones
Water alone keeps it soluble; excess phospholipids cause stones
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: Bile salts + phospholipids (lecithin) keep cholesterol dissolved; excess cholesterol (or ↓bile salts) → cholesterol precipitates → gallstones
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: Bile salts + phospholipids (lecithin) keep cholesterol dissolved. If cholesterol is in excess (or bile salts fall), cholesterol precipitates → gallstones.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: What triggers gallbladder emptying, and what causes biliary colic?
options: Secretin triggers emptying; colic from acid reflux
Gastrin triggers emptying; colic from gastritis
Motilin triggers emptying; colic from the MMC

A fatty meal → CCK → gallbladder contracts + sphincter of Oddi relaxes; a stone obstructing the cystic/common bile duct causes pain when the gallbladder contracts (biliary colic, worse after fatty meals)
The gallbladder empties continuously; colic is unrelated to meals
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: A fatty meal → CCK → gallbladder contracts + sphincter of Oddi relaxes; a stone obstructing the cystic/common bile duct causes pain when the gallbladder contracts (biliary colic, worse after fatty meals)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: A fatty meal releases CCK → gallbladder contracts and the sphincter of Oddi relaxes, delivering bile. A gallstone obstructing the cystic/common bile duct causes biliary colic — pain when the gallbladder contracts against the obstruction, especially after fatty (CCK-stimulating) meals.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: Why are bile salts able to emulsify fat, and what do they form to ferry fat-breakdown products?
options: They are amphipathic (water- and fat-soluble ends), emulsifying fat into small droplets and forming micelles that carry fat-breakdown products to the enterocyte
They are purely lipid-soluble; they form chylomicrons
They are purely water-soluble; they form triglycerides
They act as enzymes digesting fat directly
They neutralise acid to allow fat digestion
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: They are amphipathic (water- and fat-soluble ends), emulsifying fat into small droplets and forming micelles that carry fat-breakdown products to the enterocyte
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: Bile salts are amphipathic, so they emulsify fat (break large globules into small droplets → more surface area for lipase) and form micelles that ferry fat-breakdown products to the enterocyte. They are essential for absorbing fat and the fat-soluble vitamins (ADEK).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: Where are bile salts reabsorbed, and how efficient is the enterohepatic circulation?
options: The duodenum; ~50% is lost each cycle
The stomach; the whole pool is excreted each meal
The terminal ileum; the pool recirculates several times per meal with only ~5% lost in faeces (replaced by new hepatic synthesis)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: The terminal ileum; the pool recirculates several times per meal with only ~5% lost in faeces (replaced by new hepatic synthesis)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: Bile salts are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum and returned to the liver via the portal vein for re-secretion. The pool recirculates several times per meal, with only ~5% lost in faeces (replaced by new hepatic synthesis).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: A patient with Crohn's disease affecting the terminal ileum develops watery diarrhoea. What is the mechanism and treatment?
options: Excess bile salts stimulate the stomach; treat with PPI
Lactase deficiency → osmotic diarrhoea; treat with lactase
Pancreatic insufficiency → steatorrhoea; treat with Creon
Gastrin excess → secretory diarrhoea; treat with octreotide
Bile salt malabsorption → bile salts spill into the colon → bile-acid diarrhoea (they irritate the colon); treat with colestyramine (binds bile acids)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: Bile salt malabsorption → bile salts spill into the colon → bile-acid diarrhoea (they irritate the colon); treat with colestyramine (binds bile acids)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: Terminal ileal disease/resection causes bile salt malabsorption → bile salts spill into the colon → bile-acid diarrhoea (colonic irritation), treated with colestyramine, which binds bile acids.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: Besides diarrhoea, what is the other consequence of a depleted bile salt pool in terminal ileal disease?
options: Fat malabsorption + increased gallstone risk (less bile salt to keep cholesterol soluble)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: Fat malabsorption + increased gallstone risk (less bile salt to keep cholesterol soluble)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: A depleted bile salt pool causes fat malabsorption and an increased gallstone risk (less bile salt to keep cholesterol soluble). Terminal ileal disease also impairs B12 absorption, as B12 and bile salts share that site.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: How does obstruction to bile flow produce jaundice and itch?
options: Unconjugated bilirubin accumulates and bile salts fall
Albumin falls, causing jaundice and itch
Conjugated bilirubin can't be excreted → obstructive jaundice (dark urine, pale stools), and bile salts back up → itch (pruritus)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: Conjugated bilirubin can't be excreted → obstructive jaundice (dark urine, pale stools), and bile salts back up → itch (pruritus)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: Blocked bile flow (gallstone, tumour) means conjugated bilirubin can't be excreted → obstructive jaundice (dark urine, pale stools), and bile salts back up → itch (pruritus).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: In Wilson's disease, which bile-related excretory defect underlies copper accumulation?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: ↓biliary copper excretion → copper accumulation
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: Bile is the route for excreting copper (among other substances the kidney can't handle). In Wilson's disease, reduced biliary copper excretion leads to copper accumulation.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: Which cells clear bacteria and debris from the portal blood as it passes through the liver?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: Kupffer cells (resident macrophages)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: Hepatocytes do the metabolic work, while Kupffer cells (resident macrophages) clear bacteria and debris from the portal blood.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.question: Which statement about the two synthetic markers of liver function is correct?
options: Albumin has a short half-life (acute marker); PT/INR has a long half-life (chronic marker)
Both have long half-lives and reflect chronic function
Both reflect hepatocyte damage rather than synthesis
Neither is affected by liver disease
Albumin has a long half-life (chronic synthetic function); PT/INR has a short half-life (acute synthetic function)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.answer: Albumin has a long half-life (chronic synthetic function); PT/INR has a short half-life (acute synthetic function)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Foundation.explanation: Albumin has a long half-life, reflecting chronic synthetic function; PT/INR has a short half-life, reflecting acute synthetic function (and rises early because factor VII has a short half-life).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.question: Which statement best describes irritable bowel syndrome?
options: A chronic inflammatory disease of the colon with mucosal ulceration
A malignant process of the large bowel
A functional bowel disorder with no identifiable structural or organic disease
A motility disorder caused by loss of myenteric ganglion cells
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.answer: A functional bowel disorder with no identifiable structural or organic disease
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.explanation: IBS is a functional bowel disorder — symptoms arise from abnormal gut functioning with no identifiable structural or organic disease.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.question: Which statement best captures how IBS should be diagnosed?
options: Exclude organic causes, then diagnose positively on symptom criteria
Diagnose by default once all tests are normal, with no criteria needed
Diagnose on a single raised faecal calprotectin
Diagnose only after colonoscopy confirms inflammation
Diagnose purely on a positive coeliac serology
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.answer: Exclude organic causes, then diagnose positively on symptom criteria
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.explanation: The central fork is: Step 1 exclude organic causes (red flags + investigations); Step 2 diagnose positively on symptom criteria. IBS is a diagnosis of exclusion but made positively, not just by default.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.question: Which set represents the IBS triad?
options: Intestinal discomfort, bowel habit change, stool abnormality
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.answer: Intestinal discomfort, bowel habit change, stool abnormality
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.explanation: The IBS triad is intestinal discomfort, bowel habit change and stool abnormality.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.question: How is IBD best described in relation to IBS?
options: A treatable mimic that must be excluded with IgA tTG
The red-flag concern in any bowel habit change
A functional disorder identical to IBS
A paraneoplastic syndrome of colorectal cancer
The organic mirror — IBS is what remains when inflammation is excluded
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.answer: The organic mirror — IBS is what remains when inflammation is excluded
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.explanation: IBD is the organic mirror of IBS — IBS is what remains when inflammation is excluded. Coeliac is the key mimic and colorectal cancer is the red-flag concern in bowel habit change.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.question: A patient describes lower abdominal cramping pain that is worse after eating and relieved by defecation. Which feature is most consistent with IBS?
options: Pain radiating to the back and constant
Pain only at night waking the patient
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.answer: Pain relieved by defecation
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.explanation: IBS abdominal pain is relieved by defecation and worse after eating, typically cramping/colicky and in the lower abdomen.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.question: Which stool-related feature is characteristic of IBS?
options: Passage of mucus with no blood
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.answer: Passage of mucus with no blood
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.explanation: IBS bloating/distension is often worse after eating and relieved partially by defecation, with passage of mucus but no blood. Pain relieved by defecation, fluctuating habit, mucus but no blood is the classic IBS pattern.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.question: What is the overall symptom pattern of IBS?
options: Chronic, relapsing, and without alarm features
Associated with profound weight loss from onset
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.answer: Chronic, relapsing, and without alarm features
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.explanation: The IBS pattern is chronic, relapsing and without alarm features: pain relieved by defecation plus a fluctuating habit without weight loss/bleeding is functional until red flags say otherwise.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.question: A 45-year-old with several years of fluctuating bowel habit now reports new rectal bleeding. How should this be interpreted?
options: A typical feature of IBS requiring only reassurance
An expected effect of a low-FODMAP diet
A red flag mandating investigation for IBD or colorectal cancer, as IBS does not cause bleeding
Evidence that confirms the IBS diagnosis
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.answer: A red flag mandating investigation for IBD or colorectal cancer, as IBS does not cause bleeding
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.explanation: Rectal bleeding is a red flag (concern: IBD, colorectal cancer). IBS does not cause rectal bleeding, so this mandates investigation for organic disease.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.question: Which group of features does IBS NOT cause, each requiring investigation if present?
options: Pain relieved by defecation and fluctuating habit
Weight loss, rectal bleeding, anaemia and nocturnal symptoms
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.answer: Weight loss, rectal bleeding, anaemia and nocturnal symptoms
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.explanation: IBS does not cause weight loss, rectal bleeding, anaemia or nocturnal symptoms. Any of these means investigating for IBD, cancer or coeliac first.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.question: What should investigation results show in true IBS, and what is their purpose?
options: Raised inflammatory markers confirming the diagnosis
Normal results — the purpose is to exclude organic mimics, not diagnose IBS itself
A positive coeliac serology confirming IBS
Abnormal results that establish IBS positively
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.answer: Normal results — the purpose is to exclude organic mimics, not diagnose IBS itself
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.explanation: All results should be normal in IBS; the purpose of investigation is to exclude organic mimics, not to diagnose IBS itself.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.question: Which investigation is described as the key IBS vs IBD discriminator?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.answer: Faecal calprotectin
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.explanation: Faecal calprotectin is the IBS vs IBD discriminator: raised = mucosal inflammation (IBD); normal = functional disorder (IBS). It is highly sensitive for active colonic inflammation.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.question: A patient with suspected IBS has a raised CRP/ESR. What does this most suggest?
options: Inflammatory bowel disease rather than IBS
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.answer: Inflammatory bowel disease rather than IBS
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.explanation: FBC + CRP/ESR are normal in IBS; raised CRP/ESR points to IBD, acting as a key discriminator. FBC also checks for anaemia (cancer, coeliac, IBD).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.question: Why is coeliac serology (IgA tTG) mandatory before diagnosing IBS?
options: It is the test that positively confirms IBS
It detects mucosal inflammation of IBD
Coeliac is a treatable mimic with an identical GI presentation
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.answer: Coeliac is a treatable mimic with an identical GI presentation
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.explanation: Coeliac serology (IgA tTG) is mandatory before diagnosing IBS because coeliac is a treatable mimic with an identical GI presentation.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.question: A woman presents with bloating and abdominal symptoms that overlap with IBS. Which test should not be missed if ovarian cancer is suspected?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.answer: CA125
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.explanation: CA125 is checked if ovarian cancer is suspected in women, because bloating and abdominal symptoms overlap with IBS — it should not be missed.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.question: What is the core diagnostic criterion for IBS?
options: ≥2 weeks of diarrhoea with raised calprotectin
≥6 months of abdominal pain/discomfort relieved by defecation OR with altered stool frequency/form, plus ≥2 supporting features
Any chronic abdominal pain with a normal colonoscopy
≥6 months of rectal bleeding with weight loss
A single episode of pain relieved by defecation
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.answer: ≥6 months of abdominal pain/discomfort relieved by defecation OR with altered stool frequency/form, plus ≥2 supporting features
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.explanation: The criterion is ≥6 months of abdominal pain/discomfort relieved by defecation OR associated with altered stool frequency or form, PLUS ≥2 supporting features.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.question: Which is a recognised supporting feature contributing to an IBS diagnosis?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.answer: Passage of mucus
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.explanation: Supporting features (≥2 required) include straining/urgency/incomplete emptying, bloating or distension, symptoms worse after eating, and passage of mucus. Bleeding, weight loss, anaemia and nocturnal symptoms are red flags, not supporting features.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.question: What is the recommended first approach in managing IBS?
options: Lifestyle and dietary measures, including a dietitian-led low-FODMAP diet
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.answer: Lifestyle and dietary measures, including a dietitian-led low-FODMAP diet
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.explanation: Lifestyle and diet come first: regular unhurried meals, adequate fluid, limiting caffeine/alcohol/fizzy drinks, adjusting fibre, and a dietitian-led low-FODMAP diet.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.question: Which dietary intervention is described as the evidence-based option for refractory IBS symptoms?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.answer: Low-FODMAP diet (dietitian-led)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.explanation: The low-FODMAP diet (dietitian-led) limits fermentable oligosaccharides, disaccharides, monosaccharides and polyols, and is the evidence-based dietary intervention for refractory symptoms.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.question: A patient with pain/spasm-predominant IBS needs first-line pharmacological treatment. Which is appropriate?
options: An antispasmodic such as mebeverine, hyoscine or peppermint oil
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.answer: An antispasmodic such as mebeverine, hyoscine or peppermint oil
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.explanation: For pain/spasm, first-line is an antispasmodic (mebeverine, hyoscine or peppermint oil).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.question: A patient with constipation-predominant IBS is to start first-line medication. Which is appropriate, and what should be avoided?
options: Bulk-forming laxative (ispaghula husk); avoid lactulose as it worsens bloating
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.answer: Bulk-forming laxative (ispaghula husk); avoid lactulose as it worsens bloating
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.explanation: For constipation, first-line is a bulk-forming laxative (ispaghula husk); lactulose should be avoided as it worsens bloating, and linaclotide is used if refractory.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.question: Which is the first-line treatment for diarrhoea-predominant IBS?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.answer: Loperamide, titrated to response
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.explanation: For diarrhoea-predominant IBS, loperamide is first-line, titrated to response.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.question: A patient with refractory IBS is started on second-line drug therapy. Which agent is preferred, and how is it dosed?
options: Amitriptyline (a low-dose TCA), preferred over an SSRI, at 10–30 mg nocte
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.answer: Amitriptyline (a low-dose TCA), preferred over an SSRI, at 10–30 mg nocte
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.explanation: Second-line is a low-dose TCA — amitriptyline, preferred over an SSRI. It modulates the gut-brain axis, reduces visceral pain and alters gut motility, used at low dose (10–30 mg nocte).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.question: Which psychological therapies have strong evidence in refractory IBS?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.answer: CBT and gut-directed hypnotherapy
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.explanation: CBT and gut-directed hypnotherapy are used for refractory IBS, with strong evidence for the psychosocial component of functional GI disease.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.question: A 28-year-old has ≥6 months of lower abdominal cramping relieved by defecation, bloating worse after eating, and passage of mucus, with no weight loss or bleeding. FBC, CRP, faecal calprotectin and IgA tTG are all normal. What is the most appropriate conclusion and initial management?
options: Refer urgently for colonoscopy for suspected cancer
Diagnose coeliac disease and start a gluten-free diet
Start full-dose amitriptyline before any lifestyle advice
Diagnose IBS positively and begin lifestyle/dietary measures including a low-FODMAP diet
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.answer: Diagnose IBS positively and begin lifestyle/dietary measures including a low-FODMAP diet
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Irritable.explanation: The patient meets the ≥6 month criterion with ≥2 supporting features, has no red flags, and has normal investigations excluding organic mimics. IBS is diagnosed positively, and first-line management is lifestyle and dietary measures including a dietitian-led low-FODMAP diet.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.question: Which best describes the pathology of Clostridioides difficile infection?
options: Autoimmune transmural inflammation from mouth to anus
Continuous mucosal inflammation from the rectum upward
Pseudomembranous colitis from toxin-mediated mucosal damage after antibiotics suppress normal gut flora
Ischaemic necrosis of the colonic mucosa
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.answer: Pseudomembranous colitis from toxin-mediated mucosal damage after antibiotics suppress normal gut flora
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.explanation: C. diff causes pseudomembranous colitis from toxin-mediated mucosal damage after broad-spectrum antibiotics suppress normal gut flora, allowing C. diff overgrowth.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.question: A hospital inpatient develops new diarrhoea after a course of broad-spectrum antibiotics. According to the core framing, what should be assumed?
options: Antibiotic-associated functional diarrhoea needing no testing
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.answer: C. diff until proven otherwise
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.explanation: The core framing is: recent broad-spectrum antibiotics + new diarrhoea, especially in hospital = C. diff until proven otherwise. C. diff toxin should also be excluded in every IBD flare with diarrhoea before escalating immunosuppression.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.question: Which antibiotic is described as the leading cause among the '4 Cs' for C. diff?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.answer: Cephalosporins
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.explanation: The 4 Cs are cephalosporins (the leading cause), ciprofloxacin (fluoroquinolones), clindamycin and co-amoxiclav.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.question: Why are PPIs an additional risk factor for C. diff infection?
options: They produce toxin A and B
They reduce the gastric acid barrier
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.answer: They reduce the gastric acid barrier
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.explanation: PPIs are an additional risk factor because they reduce the gastric acid barrier. Others include advanced age, hospitalisation/healthcare exposure and immunosuppression.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.question: Which toxins mediate the mucosal damage in C. diff infection?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.answer: Toxin A (enterotoxin) and toxin B (cytotoxin)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.explanation: The mechanism is antibiotics → flora suppression → C. diff overgrows → toxin A (enterotoxin) + toxin B (cytotoxin) → mucosal damage → pseudomembranous colitis.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.question: Which presentation is typical of C. diff infection?
options: Painless bloody diarrhoea with weight loss
Profuse, foul-smelling diarrhoea with fever and raised WCC
Tenesmus with mucus but no diarrhoea
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.answer: Profuse, foul-smelling diarrhoea with fever and raised WCC
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.explanation: The typical presentation is profuse, foul-smelling diarrhoea, diffuse abdominal pain/cramping, fever, raised WCC (leukocytosis), dehydration and recent antibiotics/hospitalisation.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.question: Which AXR finding is described as the imaging clue in severe C. diff infection?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.answer: Thumbprinting (mucosal oedema)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.explanation: The imaging clue in severe disease is thumbprinting (mucosal oedema) on AXR. Severe/life-threatening features include toxic megacolon, ileus, perforation and hypotension/shock.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.question: A patient has a WCC of 18 ×10⁹/L, temperature 39°C and a creatinine rise of 60%. How is this C. diff episode classified?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.answer: Severe
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.explanation: Severe C. diff is WCC >15 ×10⁹/L with temp >38.5°C or creatinine ↑>50%. The key threshold is WCC >15 or AKI = severe — escalate early.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.question: Which combination of features defines life-threatening C. diff infection?
options: Normal WCC with no systemic upset
Hypotension, ileus or toxic megacolon (any WCC)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.answer: Hypotension, ileus or toxic megacolon (any WCC)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.explanation: Life-threatening C. diff is defined by hypotension, ileus or toxic megacolon at any WCC, and is treated with oral vancomycin + IV metronidazole ± colectomy.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.question: What is the gold-standard diagnostic test for C. diff, and what does it detect?
options: GDH antigen — detects the organism only
Stool C. diff toxin (CDT) — detects toxin A & B
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.answer: Stool C. diff toxin (CDT) — detects toxin A & B
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.explanation: Stool C. diff toxin (CDT) is the gold standard and detects toxin A & B. GDH antigen is a sensitive screening test; if positive, confirm with the toxin assay.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.question: A patient's stool is GDH antigen positive but C. diff toxin negative. What does this indicate, and what is the consequence?
options: A false-negative GDH that should be repeated
Colonisation, not infection — treating it is a recognised error
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.answer: Colonisation, not infection — treating it is a recognised error
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.explanation: GDH+/toxin- = colonisation, not infection. You must detect toxin — treating colonisation is a recognised error.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.question: Which severity marker specifically flags severity through acute kidney injury in C. diff?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.answer: U&E / creatinine
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.explanation: U&E/creatinine flags severity via AKI. FBC (WCC) is the severity threshold, CRP is elevated in active disease, AXR shows toxic megacolon/thumbprinting/ileus if severe, and CT abdomen is used if perforation is suspected.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.question: What is the first step and first-line treatment for a first episode of C. diff infection?
options: Stop the offending antibiotic and give oral vancomycin 125 mg QDS × 10 days
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.answer: Stop the offending antibiotic and give oral vancomycin 125 mg QDS × 10 days
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.explanation: First, stop the offending antibiotic where possible. First-line treatment is oral vancomycin 125 mg QDS × 10 days.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.question: What is the second-line treatment for a first episode of C. diff infection?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.answer: Oral fidaxomicin 200 mg BD × 10 days
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.explanation: Second-line for a first episode is oral fidaxomicin 200 mg BD × 10 days.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.question: How is life-threatening C. diff treated?
options: Oral vancomycin 500 mg QDS + IV metronidazole
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.answer: Oral vancomycin 500 mg QDS + IV metronidazole
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.explanation: Life-threatening disease is treated with oral vancomycin 500 mg QDS + IV metronidazole, with urgent surgical review (colectomy); severe (non-life-threatening) first-episode disease still uses oral vancomycin 125 mg QDS.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.question: A patient has a recurrence of C. diff 6 weeks after their first episode. What is the appropriate treatment?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.answer: Oral fidaxomicin
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.explanation: For recurrence within 12 weeks, oral fidaxomicin is used. After 12 weeks, either oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin is appropriate.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.question: A patient has had multiple recurrences of C. diff despite appropriate antibiotic courses. What is the recommended option?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.answer: Faecal microbiota transplant (FMT)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.explanation: For multiple recurrences, faecal microbiota transplant (FMT) is recommended.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.question: Why is soap-and-water handwashing emphasised over alcohol gel for C. diff infection control?
options: Soap is more convenient on wards
C. diff spores resist alcohol gel
Alcohol gel causes skin reactions in carriers
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.answer: C. diff spores resist alcohol gel
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.explanation: Soap-and-water handwashing is emphasised because C. diff spores resist alcohol gel. Other measures include single-room isolation with contact precautions, a dedicated toilet, PPE for all contacts, and antibiotic stewardship limiting the 4 Cs.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.question: Regarding current first-line treatment for C. diff, which statement is correct?
options: Fidaxomicin is first-line for every first episode
FMT is first-line for a first episode
Oral vancomycin is first-line; metronidazole is no longer first-line
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.answer: Oral vancomycin is first-line; metronidazole is no longer first-line
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.explanation: The updated guideline trap: metronidazole is no longer first-line. Current NICE guidance makes oral vancomycin first-line; older question banks may still say metronidazole.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.question: A 78-year-old inpatient on a PPI develops profuse foul-smelling diarrhoea 5 days after starting cephalosporins. WCC is 12 ×10⁹/L, creatinine is normal, and they have 4 loose stools/day with no hypotension. Stool toxin is positive. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Stop the cephalosporin where possible and start oral vancomycin
Proceed directly to faecal microbiota transplant
Treat as colonisation and give no antibiotics
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.answer: Stop the cephalosporin where possible and start oral vancomycin
