conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.explanation: This is a toxin-positive first episode of moderate severity (WCC <15, no systemic upset/AKI/hypotension). Management is to stop the offending antibiotic where possible and give oral vancomycin (first-line).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.question: A patient with confirmed C. diff deteriorates with hypotension, a silent abdomen and a colon measuring >6 cm on AXR. What is the appropriate management?
options: Oral vancomycin + IV metronidazole with surgical review for possible colectomy
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.answer: Oral vancomycin + IV metronidazole with surgical review for possible colectomy
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.explanation: Hypotension, ileus (silent abdomen) and toxic megacolon (colon >6 cm) indicate life-threatening C. diff, managed with oral vancomycin + IV metronidazole ± colectomy, with surgical review.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.question: A patient with known ulcerative colitis presents with a diarrhoeal flare after recent antibiotics. What must be done before escalating immunosuppression?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.answer: Exclude C. diff toxin
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__C. Diffici.explanation: C. diff toxin must be excluded in every IBD flare with diarrhoea before escalating immunosuppression, as recent antibiotics raise the risk of C. diff.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.question: What is the core fork that classifies bowel obstruction?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.answer: Mechanical (dynamic) vs non-mechanical (adynamic)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.explanation: The core fork is mechanical (dynamic) — physical blockage of the lumen — vs non-mechanical (adynamic) — failure of peristalsis with no structural block.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.question: Which proportions correctly describe small vs large bowel obstruction within mechanical obstruction?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.answer: SBO 80%, LBO 20%
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.explanation: Within mechanical obstruction, SBO accounts for 80% and LBO 20%.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.question: Which are the two non-mechanical (adynamic) subtypes of bowel obstruction?
options: Small bowel obstruction and large bowel obstruction
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.answer: Paralytic ileus (pan-intestinal) and pseudo-obstruction / Ogilvie's (colonic)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.explanation: The non-mechanical (adynamic) subtypes are paralytic ileus (pan-intestinal) and pseudo-obstruction / Ogilvie's (colonic).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.question: Why do patients with bowel obstruction become hypovolaemic?
options: Blood loss into the bowel lumen
Dilation causes the gut to secrete electrolyte-rich fluid, leading to third-spacing
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.answer: Dilation causes the gut to secrete electrolyte-rich fluid, leading to third-spacing
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.explanation: Blockage → dilation → the gut secretes electrolyte-rich fluid → third-spacing → hypovolaemia. Higher obstruction means greater fluid loss as there is less bowel to reabsorb.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.question: How does a proximal obstruction differ from a distal obstruction in presentation?
options: Proximal: late vomiting, early distension; distal: early vomiting, late distension
Proximal: early vomiting, late distension; distal: late vomiting, early/marked distension
Proximal: no vomiting; distal: no distension
Proximal: bloody vomiting; distal: faeculent vomiting only
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.answer: Proximal: early vomiting, late distension; distal: late vomiting, early/marked distension
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.explanation: Proximal obstruction causes early vomiting and late distension; distal obstruction causes late vomiting and early/marked distension.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.question: What defines a closed-loop obstruction, and why is it dangerous?
options: A single point of obstruction that resolves spontaneously
Failure of peristalsis with no structural block
A partial obstruction allowing some flow
Obstruction at two points simultaneously, with the trapped segment expanding to rapid ischaemia, necrosis and perforation
Obstruction relieved by an incompetent ileocaecal valve
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.answer: Obstruction at two points simultaneously, with the trapped segment expanding to rapid ischaemia, necrosis and perforation
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.explanation: Closed-loop obstruction is obstruction at two points simultaneously; the trapped segment expands, leading to rapid ischaemia → necrosis → perforation.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.question: In a large bowel obstruction with a competent ileocaecal valve, where does blowout (perforation) typically occur, and why?
options: The caecum — largest diameter gives the highest wall tension by Laplace's law
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.answer: The caecum — largest diameter gives the highest wall tension by Laplace's law
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.explanation: Blowout occurs at the caecum because its largest diameter gives the highest wall tension (Laplace's law). An LBO with a competent ileocaecal valve creates a closed loop.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.question: What is the commonest cause of small bowel obstruction?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.answer: Adhesions
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.explanation: Adhesions are the commonest cause of SBO (post-surgery, peritonitis, endometriosis). Other causes include hernias, malignancy, intussusception and Crohn's stricture.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.question: What is the commonest cause of large bowel obstruction?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.answer: Malignancy (~60%)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.explanation: Malignancy is the commonest cause of LBO (~60%), followed by diverticular stricture (~20%), volvulus (~5%) and pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie's).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.question: Which cause of bowel obstruction is classified as intraluminal?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.answer: Gallstone ileus
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.explanation: Intraluminal causes include gallstone ileus, foreign body and faecal impaction. Cancer/strictures/intussusception are intramural, and adhesions/hernias/peritoneal mets/volvulus are extramural.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.question: Which are the cardinal four symptoms of bowel obstruction?
options: Bloody diarrhoea, fever, weight loss, tenesmus
Postprandial pain, weight loss, bruit, anorexia
Rectal bleeding, mucus PR, urgency, anaemia
Colicky pain, vomiting, abdominal distension, absolute constipation
Pain out of proportion, lactic acidosis, AF, shock
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.answer: Colicky pain, vomiting, abdominal distension, absolute constipation
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.explanation: The cardinal four are colicky/crampy abdominal pain, vomiting (bilious/green), abdominal distension and absolute constipation (no stool or flatus).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.question: What does 'absolute constipation' mean in bowel obstruction?
options: No passage of stool or flatus
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.answer: No passage of stool or flatus
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.explanation: Absolute constipation means no stool or flatus is passed, and is one of the cardinal four features.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.question: On examination of a patient with bowel obstruction, which finding is a red flag for developing ischaemia?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.answer: Guarding / rebound tenderness
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.explanation: Guarding/rebound suggests developing ischaemia and is a red flag. Tympanic percussion and tinkling bowel sounds are typical examination findings of obstruction.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.question: A patient with bowel obstruction and persistent vomiting has a VBG showing metabolic alkalosis with a raised lactate. What does the raised lactate indicate?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.answer: Ischaemia
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.explanation: VBG typically shows metabolic alkalosis from vomiting; a raised lactate indicates ischaemia. A raised urea:creatinine ratio reflects dehydration/AKI.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.question: What is the imaging modality of choice in bowel obstruction?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.answer: CT abdo-pelvis + IV contrast
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.explanation: CT abdo-pelvis + IV contrast is the modality of choice, showing site, cause, ischaemia and mets. Erect CXR shows pneumoperitoneum.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.question: On AXR, which diameter thresholds distinguish small from large bowel obstruction?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.answer: SBO >3 cm; LBO >6 cm (caecum >9 cm)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.explanation: On AXR, SBO is >3 cm and LBO is >6 cm (caecum >9 cm). SBO loops are central; LBO loops are peripheral/frame.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.question: Which mucosal-fold feature on AXR indicates small bowel obstruction?
options: Valvulae conniventes crossing the entire lumen
Haustra not crossing the full lumen
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.answer: Valvulae conniventes crossing the entire lumen
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.explanation: In SBO, valvulae conniventes cross the entire lumen; in LBO, haustra do not cross the full lumen.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.question: What does the conservative 'drip & suck' management of bowel obstruction involve?
options: IV fluids with electrolyte correction, plus NBM and an NG tube to decompress the stomach
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.answer: IV fluids with electrolyte correction, plus NBM and an NG tube to decompress the stomach
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.explanation: 'Drip & suck' is IV fluids + electrolyte correction (especially K+) and NBM + NG tube to decompress the stomach, with a urinary catheter, strict fluid balance and Gastrografin at 24h.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.question: Approximately what proportion of adhesional small bowel obstruction resolves with conservative management?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.explanation: Adhesional SBO resolves conservatively in approximately 80% of cases.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.question: Which scenario is a surgical indication in bowel obstruction?
options: Adhesional SBO improving on conservative management
Suspected ischaemia with guarding, rebound and a raised lactate
Mild distension with passage of flatus
A single dose of antiemetic relieving vomiting
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.answer: Suspected ischaemia with guarding, rebound and a raised lactate
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.explanation: Surgical indications include suspected ischaemia (guarding, rebound, ↑ lactate), closed-loop obstruction, an underlying cause needing surgery, failure of conservative management at 48h, and a 'virgin abdomen'.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.question: A patient with bowel obstruction has never had abdominal surgery (a 'virgin abdomen'). Why does this prompt early surgical exploration?
options: Adhesions are the most likely cause
Ischaemia is impossible without prior surgery
Adhesions are unlikely, so a structural cause is likely
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.answer: Adhesions are unlikely, so a structural cause is likely
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.explanation: A 'virgin abdomen' (no prior surgery) makes adhesions unlikely, so a structural cause is likely, prompting early exploration.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.question: A 65-year-old with previous appendicectomy presents with colicky central abdominal pain, bilious vomiting, distension and absolute constipation. AXR shows central loops >3 cm with valvulae conniventes crossing the lumen. The abdomen is soft with no peritonism and lactate is normal. What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Conservative 'drip & suck' with NG tube and IV fluids
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.answer: Conservative 'drip & suck' with NG tube and IV fluids
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.explanation: The features and AXR indicate adhesional SBO (central loops >3 cm, valvulae conniventes), and prior surgery makes adhesions likely. With no ischaemia (soft abdomen, normal lactate), initial management is conservative 'drip & suck', which resolves ~80% of adhesional SBO.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.question: A patient with large bowel obstruction develops guarding and rebound with a rising lactate, and CT shows a closed-loop with caecal distension. What is the most appropriate management?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.answer: Urgent surgery
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Bowel Obst.explanation: Suspected ischaemia (guarding, rebound, rising lactate) and closed-loop obstruction are both surgical indications, so urgent surgery is required rather than continued conservative management.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.question: Which process describes the development of most colorectal cancers?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.explanation: Colorectal cancer arises from epithelial cells as adenocarcinoma via the adenoma–carcinoma sequence (normal mucosa → adenoma → cancer over ~10–15 years); 75% are sporadic.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.question: Which gene is mutated in familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP)?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.explanation: FAP is caused by the APC tumour suppressor gene (autosomal dominant). Lynch/HNPCC involves DNA mismatch repair genes (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.question: Which feature distinguishes FAP from Lynch syndrome?
options: FAP tumours arise in isolation; Lynch floods with polyps
FAP is autosomal recessive; Lynch is autosomal dominant
FAP floods the large intestine with 100s–1000s of polyps; Lynch tumours arise in isolation
FAP involves mismatch repair genes; Lynch involves APC
FAP causes endometrial and ovarian cancer; Lynch does not
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.answer: FAP floods the large intestine with 100s–1000s of polyps; Lynch tumours arise in isolation
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.explanation: FAP floods the large intestine with 100s–1000s of polyps (inevitable cancer usually <40); Lynch has no polyps, with tumours arising in isolation and increased CRC plus other cancers (endometrial, ovarian, gastric).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.question: What is the recommended prophylaxis for a patient with FAP?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.explanation: FAP prophylaxis is panproctocolectomy because cancer is inevitable, usually before age 40. Lynch is managed with surveillance colonoscopy.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.question: Which malignancies, besides colorectal cancer, are associated with Lynch syndrome?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.explanation: Lynch syndrome is associated with increased CRC and other cancers — endometrial, ovarian and gastric.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.question: Which sequence represents the molecular pathway of colorectal carcinogenesis?
options: p53 loss → KRAS activation → APC mutation
KRAS activation → APC mutation → p53 loss
APC mutation → p53 loss → KRAS activation
APC mutation → KRAS activation → p53 loss
MLH1 loss → APC mutation → KRAS activation
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.answer: APC mutation → KRAS activation → p53 loss
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.explanation: The molecular sequence is APC mutation (initiation) → KRAS activation → p53 loss (invasion).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.question: A patient has a right-sided (caecal) colorectal cancer. Which presentation is most characteristic, and why?
options: Iron-deficiency anaemia and a palpable RIF mass, presenting late due to a wide lumen
Early obstruction due to a narrow lumen
Mucus PR with change in bowel habit
Bright-red PR bleeding with no anaemia
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.answer: Iron-deficiency anaemia and a palpable RIF mass, presenting late due to a wide lumen
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.explanation: Right-sided (caecum/ascending) tumours have a wide lumen so present late, with iron-deficiency anaemia, abdominal pain and a palpable RIF mass.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.question: A patient with a left-sided (sigmoid) tumour is most likely to present with which hallmark?
options: Rectal bleeding, change in bowel habit and tenesmus, obstructing earlier
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.answer: Rectal bleeding, change in bowel habit and tenesmus, obstructing earlier
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.explanation: Left-sided (descending/sigmoid/rectum) tumours have a narrow lumen and obstruct earlier, with rectal bleeding, change in bowel habit, tenesmus and mucus PR.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.question: Which differential typically presents with bright-red PR blood but no change in bowel habit, weight loss or anaemia?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.explanation: Haemorrhoids cause bright-red PR blood with no habit change, weight loss or anaemia. Diverticular disease causes pain + habit change in the same age group (always exclude CRC); IBD presents younger with bloody diarrhoea.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.question: What is the NHS bowel screening test, and who is screened?
options: FIT (faecal immunochemical test) every 2 years, ages 50–74
CEA blood test every 2 years from age 60
CT colonography every 5 years from age 55
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.answer: FIT (faecal immunochemical test) every 2 years, ages 50–74
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.explanation: NHS bowel screening uses the FIT test (measures human Hb) every 2 years, ages 60–75. FIT replaced FOB, which gave false positives from dietary red meat.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.question: Why was the FIT test introduced to replace the FOB test for bowel screening?
options: FOB measured CEA rather than Hb
FOB gave false positives from dietary red meat
FOB could only be used over age 75
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.answer: FOB gave false positives from dietary red meat
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.explanation: FIT (which measures human Hb) replaced FOB because FOB gave false positives from dietary red meat.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.question: A 52-year-old presents with unexplained rectal bleeding. Which 2-week-wait criterion does this meet?
options: ≥40 with weight loss and abdominal pain
≥60 with IDA or change in bowel habit
It does not meet any 2WW criterion
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.explanation: The 2WW criteria include ≥50 with unexplained rectal bleeding, ≥40 with weight loss AND abdominal pain, ≥60 with IDA OR change in bowel habit, and a positive FIT at any age.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.question: A patient has unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia. What does the 2WW 'top and tail' approach involve?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.explanation: Unexplained IDA triggers a 2WW 'top and tail' = colonoscopy + gastroscopy.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.question: What is the gold-standard diagnostic investigation for colorectal cancer?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.explanation: Colonoscopy + biopsy is the gold standard. CT colonography is used if frail/colonoscopy intolerant, and flexible sigmoidoscopy if the only symptom is rectal bleeding.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.question: Which investigation is used specifically for rectal cancers to assess depth of invasion and the mesorectal fascia?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.explanation: MRI rectum is used for rectal cancers only, assessing depth of invasion and the mesorectal fascia. CT chest-abdomen-pelvis stages all CRC; endoanal USS assesses early rectal (T1/T2) disease.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.question: What is the role of CEA in colorectal cancer?
options: A screening test in the general population
Used to assess depth of invasion
Not diagnostic — used to monitor recurrence
Used to grade the tumour histologically
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.answer: Not diagnostic — used to monitor recurrence
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.explanation: CEA is not diagnostic; it is used to monitor recurrence.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.question: In TNM staging of colorectal cancer, what does a T2 tumour involve?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.explanation: T1 is submucosa, T2 is muscularis propria, T3 is subserosa/perirectal fat, and T4a/b is through serosa / into adjacent organs.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.question: Which Dukes stage corresponds to lymph node involvement, and what is its approximate 5-year survival?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.explanation: Dukes C is lymph node involvement (~30% 5-yr survival). A is confined to the bowel wall (~90%), B is through the wall with no nodes (~65%), and D is distant metastases (<10%).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.question: Which Dukes stage corresponds to distant metastases?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.explanation: Dukes D is distant metastases with a 5-year survival of <10%.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.question: Which operation is appropriate for a caecal (right-sided) colon cancer?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.explanation: Caecum/ascending/proximal transverse cancers are treated with a right hemicolectomy (ileo-colic anastomosis).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.question: A patient has a low rectal cancer 3 cm from the anal verge. Which operation is appropriate, and what is the outcome?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.explanation: A low rectal cancer <5 cm from the anus requires an abdominoperineal resection (APR) with a permanent end colostomy. A tumour >5 cm can have a sphincter-sparing low anterior resection (LAR).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.question: A patient has a low rectal cancer 7 cm from the anus. Which operation preserves the sphincter?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.explanation: A low rectal cancer >5 cm from the anus is treated with a sphincter-sparing low anterior resection (LAR), with colo-rectal anastomosis ± defunctioning stoma. APR (permanent colostomy) is reserved for tumours <5 cm.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.question: Which operation is used for an obstructing colorectal cancer presenting as an emergency?
options: Right hemicolectomy with primary anastomosis only
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.explanation: In the emergency setting, Hartmann's procedure is used, with an end colostomy that is reversible.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.question: Why is neoadjuvant radiotherapy used for rectal cancer but not colon cancer?
options: The colon is extraperitoneal and safe to irradiate; the rectum is mobile
Colon cancer is always metastatic at diagnosis
Rectal cancer never responds to chemotherapy
The colon has no blood supply to support irradiation
The rectum is extraperitoneal and safe to irradiate; the colon is intraperitoneal and mobile
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.answer: The rectum is extraperitoneal and safe to irradiate; the colon is intraperitoneal and mobile
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.explanation: Radiotherapy is for rectal cancer only (neoadjuvant, pre-op) because the rectum is extraperitoneal and safe to irradiate, whereas the colon is intraperitoneal and mobile and cannot be safely irradiated.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.question: A 68-year-old presents with iron-deficiency anaemia, vague abdominal pain and a palpable mass in the right iliac fossa. Colonoscopy + biopsy confirms adenocarcinoma of the caecum, and CT shows no metastases. Which single statement best fits this case?
options: This is a left-sided cancer presenting with early obstruction
This is a right-sided cancer (wide lumen, presents late); treat with right hemicolectomy
CEA should be used to confirm the diagnosis
Radiotherapy is the mainstay as for rectal tumours
Abdominoperineal resection is the operation of choice
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.answer: This is a right-sided cancer (wide lumen, presents late); treat with right hemicolectomy
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Colorectal.explanation: Iron-deficiency anaemia with a palpable RIF mass reflects a right-sided (caecal) cancer, which presents late due to a wide lumen. The operation is a right hemicolectomy. CEA is not diagnostic, and radiotherapy is reserved for rectal tumours.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.question: What best describes a stoma?
options: An internal anastomosis between two loops of bowel
A narrowing of the bowel lumen from scarring
A fistula between bowel and bladder
An artificial opening of bowel or urinary system onto the abdominal surface, bypassing distal portions
A pouch fashioned entirely inside the abdomen
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.answer: An artificial opening of bowel or urinary system onto the abdominal surface, bypassing distal portions
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.explanation: A stoma is an artificial opening of the bowel or urinary system onto the abdominal surface; a bag collects waste, bypassing distal portions of the tract.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.question: Which feature correctly describes the output of an ileostomy compared with a colostomy?
options: Ileostomy output is more liquid because reabsorption occurs downstream in the bypassed colon
Ileostomy output is more solid because water is already reabsorbed
Colostomy output is more liquid than ileostomy output
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.answer: Ileostomy output is more liquid because reabsorption occurs downstream in the bypassed colon
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.explanation: An ileostomy brings out the ileum, so output is more liquid because reabsorption normally occurs downstream in the colon, which is bypassed. A colostomy output is more solid as water is already reabsorbed.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.question: Why is an ileostomy spouted rather than flat to the skin?
options: The solid output is not irritant
The liquid output is irritant and must drain clear of the skin
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.answer: The liquid output is irritant and must drain clear of the skin
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.explanation: An ileostomy is spouted because the liquid output is irritant and must drain clear of the skin. A colostomy is flat to the skin because its solid output is not irritant.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.question: What is the typical site of a colostomy versus an ileostomy?
options: Colostomy in the RIF; ileostomy in the LIF
Colostomy in the LIF; ileostomy in the RIF
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.answer: Colostomy in the LIF; ileostomy in the RIF
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.explanation: A colostomy typically sits in the LIF (solid, flat) and an ileostomy in the RIF (irritant liquid, spouted).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.question: A stoma in the right iliac fossa is spouted with liquid output. Which type is it most likely to be?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.answer: Ileostomy
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.explanation: An RIF, spouted stoma with irritant liquid output is an ileostomy (memory hook: ileostomy = irritant liquid → needs a spout, sits in RIF).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.question: How is an end stoma made?
options: The bowel is partially opened and folded to give two openings side-by-side
Two separate loops are brought out at different sites
The stomach is connected to the abdominal wall
The proximal cut end is brought to the skin; the distal end is sutured closed inside the abdomen
The ureters are anastomosed to an ileal segment
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.answer: The proximal cut end is brought to the skin; the distal end is sutured closed inside the abdomen
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.explanation: An end stoma is made by bringing the proximal cut end to the skin and suturing the distal end closed inside the abdomen, typically after resection of a bowel segment.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.question: What is the purpose of a loop stoma?
options: To defunction a distal anastomosis and let it heal
To deliver feed directly to the stomach
To remove the rectum and anus
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.answer: To defunction a distal anastomosis and let it heal
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.explanation: A loop stoma is bowel partially opened and folded to give two openings side-by-side, made to defunction a distal anastomosis (let it heal).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.question: When is a loop stoma typically reversed?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.answer: At 6–8 weeks
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.explanation: A loop stoma is reversible and typically reversed at 6–8 weeks. An end stoma is sometimes reversible if the distal end is preserved.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.question: Why is an end colostomy permanent after an abdominoperineal resection (APR)?
options: The distal end is preserved for later reversal
The colon is too liquid to reconnect
It is defunctioning a distal anastomosis
It can be reversed at 6–8 weeks
The rectum and anus are removed, making reversal impossible
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.answer: The rectum and anus are removed, making reversal impossible
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.explanation: An end colostomy is permanent after APR because the rectum and anus are removed, so reversal is impossible. It sits in the lower left abdomen (LIF).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.question: A patient has an end ileostomy after panproctocolectomy for FAP. What is an alternative that avoids a permanent stoma?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.answer: A J-pouch (ileo-anal anastomosis)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.explanation: An end ileostomy is permanent after panproctocolectomy (IBD, FAP); the alternative is a J-pouch (ileo-anal anastomosis), which avoids a permanent stoma.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.question: What is the function of a gastrostomy?
options: Draining bowel contents into a bag
Delivering feed directly when oral nutrition is not possible
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.answer: Delivering feed directly when oral nutrition is not possible
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.explanation: A gastrostomy is an artificial connection between the stomach and abdominal wall that delivers feed directly when oral nutrition is not possible (feeding, not draining).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.question: How is a PEG (percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy) fitted, and what is a typical indication?
options: Fitted endoscopically; for neurological dysphagia such as stroke or MND
Fitted surgically; to defunction an anastomosis
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.answer: Fitted endoscopically; for neurological dysphagia such as stroke or MND
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.explanation: A PEG is fitted endoscopically. Indications include neurological dysphagia (stroke, MND) and head/neck cancer.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.question: After which operation is a urostomy (ileal conduit) indicated?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.answer: Cystectomy (bladder removal)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.explanation: A urostomy (ileal conduit) is indicated after cystectomy. Urine bypasses the ureters, bladder and urethra, and the stoma is spouted and sited in the RIF.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.question: How is a urostomy (ileal conduit) constructed?
options: The colon is brought directly to the skin
The stomach is connected to the abdominal wall
The bladder is brought out as a stoma
Two loops of ileum are folded side-by-side
15–20 cm of ileum is isolated, the ureters are anastomosed to it, and the distal end is brought to the skin
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.answer: 15–20 cm of ileum is isolated, the ureters are anastomosed to it, and the distal end is brought to the skin
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.explanation: In an ileal conduit, 15–20 cm of ileum is isolated (remaining bowel re-anastomosed), the ureters are anastomosed to the isolated ileal segment, and the distal end is brought to the skin as a stoma so urine drains into a bag.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.question: A patient's stoma develops bowel herniating through the abdominal wall defect around it. Which complication is this?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.answer: Parastomal hernia
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.explanation: A parastomal hernia is bowel herniating through the defect. Prolapse is bowel telescoping through, retraction is sinking below skin (leak risk), and granulomas are raised red lumps at the stoma margin.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.question: A patient's stoma has sunk below the skin level, raising the risk of leakage. Which mechanical complication is this?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.answer: Retraction
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.explanation: Retraction is when the stoma sinks below the skin, carrying a leak risk.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.question: Which is the key metabolic complication of a high-output ileostomy?
options: Dehydration with electrolyte loss (Na+, K+, Mg2+) leading to AKI
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.answer: Dehydration with electrolyte loss (Na+, K+, Mg2+) leading to AKI
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.explanation: A high-output ileostomy causes dehydration and electrolyte loss (Na+, K+, Mg2+) leading to AKI — the key metabolic complication.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.question: Which functional complication is particularly associated with colostomies?
options: Peristomal skin irritation from irritant liquid
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.answer: Constipation
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.explanation: Constipation is listed as a functional complication of colostomies. High-output dehydration and severe skin irritation are more associated with ileostomies/urostomies.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.question: A 30-year-old with ulcerative colitis undergoes panproctocolectomy and has a stoma in the right iliac fossa with spouted, liquid output. Which stoma is this, and is it reversible?
options: An end colostomy — permanent after APR
A loop ileostomy — reversed at 6–8 weeks
An end ileostomy — permanent, though a J-pouch is an alternative that avoids a permanent stoma
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.answer: An end ileostomy — permanent, though a J-pouch is an alternative that avoids a permanent stoma
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.explanation: An RIF, spouted, liquid-output stoma after panproctocolectomy is an end ileostomy, which is permanent. A J-pouch (ileo-anal anastomosis) is the alternative that avoids a permanent stoma.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.question: A patient with a new ileostomy is producing very high volumes of liquid effluent and becomes drowsy with a rising creatinine. Which complication and mechanism best explain this?
options: High-output ileostomy causing dehydration and electrolyte loss leading to AKI
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.answer: High-output ileostomy causing dehydration and electrolyte loss leading to AKI
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Stomas (ty.explanation: A high-output ileostomy causes dehydration and electrolyte loss (Na+, K+, Mg2+), leading to AKI — consistent with high effluent volumes, drowsiness and a rising creatinine.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.question: Where are colonic diverticula most commonly found?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.explanation: Diverticula are outpouchings of colonic mucosa through weak points in the bowel wall, commonest in the sigmoid colon.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.question: Which stage of the diverticular spectrum is asymptomatic and typically an incidental finding?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.explanation: Diverticulosis means pouches are present and it is asymptomatic — an incidental finding. Diverticular disease is symptomatic pouches; diverticulitis is inflamed/infected pouches.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.question: Which presentation defines a diverticular bleed?
options: LIF pain with fever and raised CRP
Intermittent LIF pain with altered bowel habit
Painless, large-volume PR bleed from vessel erosion
Bloody diarrhoea with mucus and tenesmus
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.answer: Painless, large-volume PR bleed from vessel erosion
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.explanation: A diverticular bleed results from vessel erosion and presents as a painless, large-volume PR bleed.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.question: Which is the key differential for diverticular disease that shares the same demographic and must always be excluded?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.explanation: Colorectal cancer is the key differential (same demographic — always exclude). IBD is distinguished by faecal calprotectin.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.question: Which mechanism best explains why diverticula form?
options: Low-fibre diet → harder stool → straining → raised intraluminal pressure, herniating mucosa at vessel entry points
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.answer: Low-fibre diet → harder stool → straining → raised intraluminal pressure, herniating mucosa at vessel entry points
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.explanation: A low-fibre diet causes harder stool and straining, raising intraluminal pressure; with an ageing bowel wall, mucosa herniates through weak points where blood vessels penetrate the circular muscle (between the taenia coli).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.question: Why do diverticula never form in the rectum?
options: It has the highest intraluminal pressure
It is lined by squamous epithelium
It has a complete outer longitudinal muscle layer and no taenia coli
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.answer: It has a complete outer longitudinal muscle layer and no taenia coli
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.explanation: Diverticula never form in the rectum because it has a complete outer longitudinal muscle layer and no taenia coli, so there are no weak points for herniation.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.question: What anatomical feature explains why diverticula bleed, and what is the clinical significance?
options: A vasa recta runs alongside each pouch; erosion causes the commonest significant lower GI haemorrhage in adults
A submucosal venous plexus surrounds each pouch, causing slow venous ooze
Lymphatic channels rupture into the lumen
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.answer: A vasa recta runs alongside each pouch; erosion causes the commonest significant lower GI haemorrhage in adults
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.explanation: A vasa recta runs directly alongside each pouch (the same anatomical weak point); erosion causes a painless, large-volume arterial PR bleed — the most common cause of significant lower GI haemorrhage in adults.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.question: Which is the key modifiable risk factor for diverticular disease?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.explanation: Low fibre is the key modifiable risk factor; others include high red meat, age, obesity and smoking. NSAIDs/steroids increase perforation risk.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.question: A patient with diverticulitis develops guarding and rebound tenderness. What does this most suggest?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.explanation: Guarding/rebound suggests complicated disease (perforation). Simple diverticulitis is inflammation only; complicated includes abscess, perforation, fistula or obstruction.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.question: Diverticulitis is sometimes described as 'left-sided appendicitis'. What does this analogy convey?
options: That it is caused by an appendicolith
The same inflammatory-then-perforation logic, on the opposite side
That it presents with RIF pain
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.answer: The same inflammatory-then-perforation logic, on the opposite side
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.explanation: 'Left-sided appendicitis' conveys the same inflammatory-then-perforation logic as appendicitis, but on the opposite side.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.question: What is the first-line imaging in acute diverticulitis, and what findings does it show?
options: Colonoscopy — to visualise the inflamed pouches directly
Barium enema — to outline the diverticula
MRI pelvis — to assess fistulae acutely
CT abdo-pelvis — bowel wall thickening, pericolonic fat stranding, abscess, free air
Abdominal ultrasound — first-line for all cases
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.answer: CT abdo-pelvis — bowel wall thickening, pericolonic fat stranding, abscess, free air
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.explanation: CT abdo-pelvis is first-line, showing bowel wall thickening, pericolonic fat stranding, abscess and free air (perforation). Erect CXR shows pneumoperitoneum if perforation is suspected.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.question: Why must colonoscopy never be performed acutely in diverticulitis, and when should it be done?
options: Perforation risk; scope after resolution (6–8 weeks) to exclude colorectal cancer
It causes bleeding; scope at 24 hours
It is painful; scope only if symptoms persist
It is unnecessary; colonoscopy is never indicated
It worsens the bleed; scope only during active bleeding
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.answer: Perforation risk; scope after resolution (6–8 weeks) to exclude colorectal cancer
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.explanation: Colonoscopy is never done acutely because of perforation risk; it is performed after resolution (6–8 weeks) to exclude colorectal cancer.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.question: Which finding on urine dip is explained by bladder irritation in diverticulitis?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.explanation: Urine dip may show leucocytes ± haematuria from bladder irritation in diverticulitis.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.question: According to the Hinchey classification, how is stage 0/Ia (mild/pericolic phlegmon) managed?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.explanation: Hinchey stage 0/Ia (mild/pericolic phlegmon) is managed with oral antibiotics as an outpatient.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.question: A patient with diverticulitis has a 6 cm pericolic abscess (Hinchey Ib/II). What is the appropriate management?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.explanation: Hinchey Ib/II (pericolic or pelvic abscess) is managed with IV antibiotics ± CT-guided drainage if >5 cm. A 6 cm abscess meets the threshold for drainage.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.question: A patient with diverticulitis develops faecal peritonitis (Hinchey IV). What is the appropriate management?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.explanation: Hinchey III (purulent peritonitis) and IV (faecal peritonitis) both require surgery — Hartmann's procedure.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.question: Which oral antibiotic is first-line for uncomplicated outpatient diverticulitis, and what is used if penicillin-allergic?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.explanation: Uncomplicated diverticulitis is treated with oral co-amoxiclav for ≥5 days (ciprofloxacin + metronidazole if penicillin-allergic).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.question: Which analgesic approach is recommended in diverticulitis, and what should be avoided?
options: Paracetamol; avoid NSAIDs (increase perforation) and opioids (mask symptoms)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.answer: Paracetamol; avoid NSAIDs (increase perforation) and opioids (mask symptoms)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.explanation: Paracetamol is used; NSAIDs are avoided because they increase perforation risk, and opioids are avoided because they mask symptoms.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.question: What does Hartmann's procedure involve in complicated diverticulitis?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.explanation: Perforation/peritonitis is managed with Hartmann's procedure — sigmoid colectomy + end colostomy, which is approximately 50% reversible.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.question: Which set of features distinguishes a diverticular bleed from diverticulitis?
options: LIF pain with fever and raised WCC/CRP
Painless, large-volume fresh PR bleed; no fever; no inflammatory response; usually self-limiting
Guarding and rebound with free air on CT
Altered bowel habit with weight loss
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.answer: Painless, large-volume fresh PR bleed; no fever; no inflammatory response; usually self-limiting
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.explanation: A diverticular bleed (vascular) is a painless, large-volume fresh PR bleed with no fever and no inflammatory response, usually self-limiting (80%). Diverticulitis (inflammatory) has LIF pain + fever with raised WCC/CRP.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.question: What is the first-line investigation in the management ladder for a diverticular bleed after resuscitation?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.explanation: Bleed management is resuscitate → CT angiography (1st-line) → endoscopic haemostasis/embolisation → surgery if refractory.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.question: A man with chronic diverticular disease presents with pneumaturia, faecaluria and recurrent UTIs. Which complication is this?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.explanation: A colovesical fistula (commonest, in men) presents with pneumaturia, faecaluria and recurrent UTIs.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.question: A woman with chronic diverticular disease reports passing faeces and flatus per vagina. Which complication does this indicate, and what does its management require?
options: Colovesical fistula — managed with antibiotics alone
Colovaginal fistula — all fistulae require surgery
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.answer: Colovaginal fistula — all fistulae require surgery
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.explanation: A colovaginal fistula presents with faeces/flatus per vagina. All fistulae require surgery.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.question: A 60-year-old presents with LIF pain worse on movement, fever and anorexia. Exam shows LIF tenderness with a palpable mass, and bloods show raised WCC and CRP. CT shows pericolonic fat stranding and a 4 cm abscess. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Discharge on oral antibiotics with outpatient review
Arrange urgent colonoscopy to confirm the diagnosis
Admit for IV antibiotics; CT-guided drainage if the abscess enlarges beyond 5 cm
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.answer: Admit for IV antibiotics; CT-guided drainage if the abscess enlarges beyond 5 cm
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.explanation: This is complicated diverticulitis with an abscess. Management is admission with IV antibiotics; CT-guided drainage is indicated for an abscess >5 cm, so a 4 cm abscess is managed with IV antibiotics with drainage reserved if it exceeds 5 cm.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.question: A 72-year-old presents with a sudden painless, large-volume fresh PR bleed. There is no abdominal pain, fever, or rise in inflammatory markers, and they are haemodynamically stabilised with fluids. What is the most appropriate next step, and what is the likely course?
options: Immediate Hartmann's procedure; the bleed rarely stops
CT angiography as first-line; the bleed is usually self-limiting (80%)
Urgent colonoscopy acutely to control the bleed
Erect CXR to look for pneumoperitoneum
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.answer: CT angiography as first-line; the bleed is usually self-limiting (80%)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Diverticul.explanation: A painless, large-volume fresh PR bleed with no inflammatory response is a diverticular bleed, usually self-limiting (80%). After resuscitation, CT angiography is first-line, followed by endoscopic haemostasis/embolisation and surgery if refractory.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: On what three features are the two types of IBD distinguished?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: Distribution, depth, and pathological pattern
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: IBD is recurrent inflammation of the GI tract; the two types — Crohn's and UC — are distinguished by distribution, depth and pathological pattern.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: Which distribution pattern is characteristic of Crohn's disease?
options: Mouth to anus with skip lesions; terminal ileum commonest
Rectum upward, continuous, never past the ileocaecal valve
Large bowel only, sparing the small bowel
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: Mouth to anus with skip lesions; terminal ileum commonest
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: Crohn's affects mouth → anus with skip lesions, terminal ileum commonest. UC is continuous from the rectum upward and never extends past the ileocaecal valve.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: Which statement about the depth of inflammation is correct?
options: Crohn's affects mucosa only; UC is transmural
Crohn's is transmural; UC affects mucosa/submucosa only
Crohn's is serosal only; UC is muscular only
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: Crohn's is transmural; UC affects mucosa/submucosa only
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: Crohn's inflammation is transmural (full thickness); UC affects mucosa/submucosa only.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: A patient presents with chronic non-bloody diarrhoea and prominent weight loss. Which IBD type does this favour?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: Crohn's disease
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: Crohn's causes non-bloody diarrhoea with prominent weight loss, whereas UC causes bloody diarrhoea + mucus with tenesmus and LLQ pain.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: Which histological finding is characteristic of Crohn's disease?
options: Crypt abscesses with goblet cell depletion
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: Granulomas with preserved goblet cells
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: Crohn's histology shows granulomas and increased goblet cells; UC shows crypt abscesses and goblet cell depletion.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: Which histological finding is characteristic of ulcerative colitis?
options: Crypt abscesses with goblet cell depletion
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: Crypt abscesses with goblet cell depletion
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: UC histology shows crypt abscesses and goblet cell depletion; granulomas and increased goblet cells are features of Crohn's.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: Which endoscopic appearance is typical of Crohn's disease?
options: Cobblestone mucosa with deep ulcers and skip lesions
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: Cobblestone mucosa with deep ulcers and skip lesions
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: Crohn's endoscopy shows cobblestone mucosa, deep ulcers and skip lesions; UC shows pseudopolyps and continuous inflammation.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: Which radiological sign is associated with ulcerative colitis?
options: Lead-pipe colon with loss of haustra
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: Lead-pipe colon with loss of haustra
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: UC radiology shows a lead-pipe colon with loss of haustra; Crohn's shows Kantor's string sign, rose-thorn ulcers and fistulae.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: How does smoking affect the two types of IBD?
options: It is protective in Crohn's but worsens UC
It has no effect on either
It worsens Crohn's but is protective in UC
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: It worsens Crohn's but is protective in UC
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: Smoking is a risk factor that worsens Crohn's, but is protective in UC — the counterintuitive classic. Smoking protects in UC and harms in Crohn's.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: Which statement about surgery in IBD is correct?
options: Surgery is curative in Crohn's but not in UC
Surgery is curative in UC (panproctocolectomy) but not in Crohn's (recurs panenterically)
Surgery is only ever used for extraintestinal disease
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: Surgery is curative in UC (panproctocolectomy) but not in Crohn's (recurs panenterically)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: In UC, panproctocolectomy removes the entire disease and is curative. In Crohn's, surgery is not curative — disease recurs at new sites (panenteric).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: A patient with IBD develops tender red nodules on the shins. What is this extraintestinal manifestation?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: Erythema nodosum
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: Erythema nodosum (tender red nodules on the shins) is a skin extraintestinal manifestation of IBD; pyoderma gangrenosum is a deep ulcerating skin lesion.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: Which extraintestinal manifestation of IBD is associated with HLA-B27?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: Ankylosing spondylitis / sacroiliitis
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: Joint manifestations include arthralgia and ankylosing spondylitis/sacroiliitis (HLA-B27).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: Why do oxalate renal stones occur specifically in Crohn's disease?
options: Increased oxalate absorption due to fat malabsorption
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: Increased oxalate absorption due to fat malabsorption
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: Oxalate renal stones occur in Crohn's because of increased oxalate absorption due to fat malabsorption.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: Which blood/stool test is described as the IBS vs IBD discriminator?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: Faecal calprotectin
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: Faecal calprotectin is the IBS vs IBD discriminator — raised in IBD (mucosal inflammation), normal in IBS.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: Why should stool cultures and C. difficile testing be done before confirming an IBD flare?
options: To confirm the diagnosis of Crohn's specifically
To exclude an infectious cause of diarrhoea, especially C. difficile if recent antibiotics
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: To exclude an infectious cause of diarrhoea, especially C. difficile if recent antibiotics
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: Stool cultures + C. difficile testing always exclude an infectious cause of diarrhoea (especially if recent antibiotics) before confirming an IBD flare.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: What is the investigation of choice for IBD, and what is the key caution in severe colitis?
options: AXR; full colonoscopy is always safe in severe colitis
MRI small bowel; biopsy is contraindicated
Barium enema; safe in all settings
Colonoscopy + biopsy; use flexi-sigmoidoscopy in severe colitis due to perforation risk
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: Colonoscopy + biopsy; use flexi-sigmoidoscopy in severe colitis due to perforation risk
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: Colonoscopy + biopsy is the investigation of choice for both; flexi-sigmoidoscopy is used in severe colitis because full colonoscopy carries a perforation risk. AXR in acute severe UC excludes toxic megacolon (>6cm transverse colon).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: A patient with Crohn's has RIF pain mimicking appendicitis, perianal fistulae and aphthous mouth ulcers. Which feature is described as pathognomonic of Crohn's?
options: Perianal disease (fistulae, skin tags, fissures, abscesses)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: Perianal disease (fistulae, skin tags, fissures, abscesses)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: Perianal disease (fistulae, skin tags, fissures, abscesses) is pathognomonic of Crohn's and may predate GI symptoms.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: Why may diarrhoea be steatorrhoeic in Crohn's with terminal ileum involvement?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: Reduced fat absorption
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: Crohn's diarrhoea is usually non-bloody but may be steatorrhoeic if there is terminal ileum involvement, due to reduced fat absorption.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: What is the first-line treatment to induce remission in mild-moderate Crohn's disease?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: Oral prednisolone (steroids)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: Steroids are first-line to induce remission in Crohn's: oral prednisolone for mild-moderate, IV hydrocortisone for severe/hospitalised, and budesonide for terminal ileal/right-sided disease.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: Which steroid is preferred for terminal ileal/right-sided Crohn's because of its topical effect and fewer systemic side effects?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: Budesonide
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: Budesonide is used for terminal ileal/right-sided disease, giving a topical effect with fewer systemic side effects.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: Before starting azathioprine in Crohn's, which enzyme activity must be checked, and why?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: TPMT — deficiency causes severe myelosuppression
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: TPMT activity must be checked before starting azathioprine/mercaptopurine: TPMT deficiency leads to severe myelosuppression — a classic prescribing SBA.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: Before starting infliximab for refractory or fistulating Crohn's, what must be screened for?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: Tuberculosis
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: Infliximab (anti-TNF) is used for refractory or fistulating disease; patients must be screened for TB before starting. Other biologics include adalimumab, ustekinumab and vedolizumab.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: Which remission-induction option is preferred over steroids in children with Crohn's disease?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: Exclusive enteral nutrition (EEN)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: Enteral nutrition is preferred over steroids in children: exclusive enteral nutrition (EEN) has equivalent efficacy to steroids with nutritional benefit and no steroid side effects.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: What is the first-line maintenance therapy (the backbone) for Crohn's disease?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: Azathioprine / mercaptopurine
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: Azathioprine/mercaptopurine is the backbone of Crohn's maintenance (methotrexate if intolerant). Second-line is methotrexate (monitor LFTs, folate supplementation) and anti-TNF biologics for persistent/severe disease.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: A patient with Crohn's develops pneumaturia. Which complication does this indicate?
options: An enterovesical fistula (tracking to the bladder)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: An enterovesical fistula (tracking to the bladder)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: Transmural inflammation can track to the bladder (enterovesical fistula → pneumaturia). Fistulae are pathognomonic of Crohn's.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: Why do cholesterol gallstones form in Crohn's with terminal ileum disease?
options: Reduced bile acid reabsorption depletes the bile acid pool
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: Reduced bile acid reabsorption depletes the bile acid pool
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: Terminal ileum disease (or resection) reduces bile-acid reabsorption, depleting the bile-acid pool. Bile then becomes supersaturated with cholesterol (lithogenic), predisposing to cholesterol gallstones.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: A patient with Crohn's strictures has a contrast study showing luminal narrowing. Which sign is described?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: Kantor's string sign
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: Fibrosis from repeated transmural inflammation causes luminal narrowing → Kantor's string sign on contrast, which can lead to bowel obstruction.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: Which statement about the distribution of ulcerative colitis is correct?
options: Patchy transmural inflammation from mouth to anus
Continuous mucosal inflammation from the rectum upward, never past the ileocaecal valve
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: Continuous mucosal inflammation from the rectum upward, never past the ileocaecal valve
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: UC is mucosal inflammation of the colon and rectum, continuous from the rectum upward, never extending past the ileocaecal valve, with bloody diarrhoea as the hallmark.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: According to Truelove-Witts criteria, which describes a severe UC flare?
options: Any number of stools with normal inflammatory markers
Bloody stools with a normal Hb and ESR
>6 bloody stools/day with fever, tachycardia, anaemia (Hb<10.5) and ESR >30
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: >6 bloody stools/day with fever, tachycardia, anaemia (Hb<10.5) and ESR >30
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: By Truelove-Witts, severe UC is >6 bloody stools/day with systemic features: fever, tachycardia, anaemia (Hb<10.5) and raised ESR (>30). Mild is <4 stools/day with no systemic features; moderate is 4–6 with minimal features.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: Which trigger can precipitate a UC flare specifically because of its loss of a protective effect?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: Stopping smoking
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: Flare triggers to avoid include stress, NSAIDs, antibiotics and stopping smoking — smoking is protective in UC, so cessation can precipitate a flare.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: What is the first-line treatment to induce remission in mild-moderate ulcerative colitis?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: Aminosalicylates (mesalazine)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: For mild-moderate UC, aminosalicylates (mesalazine) are first-line (oral ± rectal); steroids (oral prednisolone) are second-line.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: Why might oral rather than rectal aminosalicylate be needed in UC extending beyond the left colon?
options: Rectal preparations only reach the splenic flexure
Rectal preparations are more systemically toxic
Oral preparations are contraindicated in proctitis
Oral preparations do not reach the colon
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: Rectal preparations only reach the splenic flexure
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: Aminosalicylates can be oral ± rectal; rectal preparations only reach the splenic flexure, so oral is used if disease is beyond the left colon.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: A patient is admitted with severe UC. What is the first-line treatment, and what is done if there is no response by day 3–5?
options: Oral mesalazine first-line; surgery if no response
Oral prednisolone first-line; azathioprine if no response
IV hydrocortisone first-line; IV ciclosporin or infliximab if no response by day 3–5
Infliximab first-line; hydrocortisone if no response
LMWH first-line; colectomy if no response
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: IV hydrocortisone first-line; IV ciclosporin or infliximab if no response by day 3–5
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: Severe UC is admitted: IV hydrocortisone is first-line; no response by day 3–5 → IV ciclosporin or infliximab. LMWH is given (high VTE risk in active colitis), colectomy if failing medical therapy, and AXR to exclude toxic megacolon.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: Why is LMWH given to patients admitted with active ulcerative colitis?
options: To treat the colonic inflammation directly
High VTE risk in active colitis
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: High VTE risk in active colitis
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: LMWH is given because there is a high VTE risk in active colitis.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: A patient on maintenance mesalazine for UC develops fever and a sore throat. What is the key concern and action?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: Agranulocytosis — check FBC
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: Aminosalicylates can cause agranulocytosis — check FBC if there is fever/sore throat (the same vigilance as carbimazole). They can also cause pancreatitis.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: What is the curative surgery for ulcerative colitis?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: Panproctocolectomy
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: Panproctocolectomy removes the entire diseased organ and cures UC. Options are a permanent ileostomy or an ileoanal (J-) pouch.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: A UC patient opts for an ileoanal pouch (J-pouch) rather than a permanent ileostomy. What is the recognised risk of this option?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: Pouchitis
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: An ileoanal pouch (J-pouch) is a reservoir fashioned from ileum and anastomosed to the anus, avoiding a permanent stoma but carrying a risk of pouchitis.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: A patient with severe UC has colonic dilatation of >6cm on AXR with systemic toxicity. What is this, and what is the management if medical therapy fails?
options: Toxic megacolon — emergency colectomy if medical therapy fails within 24–48h
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: Toxic megacolon — emergency colectomy if medical therapy fails within 24–48h
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: Toxic megacolon is colonic dilatation >6cm on AXR with systemic toxicity — life-threatening. Emergency colectomy is performed if medical therapy fails within 24–48h.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: Which factors increase the colorectal cancer risk in ulcerative colitis, and how is it monitored?
options: Smoking and short disease duration; annual CT
Terminal ileal disease; barium enema every 10 years
Family history alone; surveillance only after symptoms
Pancolitis, long disease duration (>10yr) and PSC; surveillance colonoscopy every 1–5 years
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: Pancolitis, long disease duration (>10yr) and PSC; surveillance colonoscopy every 1–5 years
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: Colorectal cancer risk is increased with pancolitis, long disease duration (>10yr) and PSC, with surveillance colonoscopy every 1–5 years depending on risk.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: A patient with UC has a raised ALP and biliary tree stricturing. Which associated condition is this, and what malignancy does it predispose to?
options: Primary biliary cholangitis — increased hepatocellular carcinoma risk
Primary sclerosing cholangitis — increased cholangiocarcinoma risk
Toxic megacolon — increased colorectal cancer risk
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: Primary sclerosing cholangitis — increased cholangiocarcinoma risk
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: PSC is the classic UC hepatic association — stricturing of the biliary tree with raised ALP and an increased cholangiocarcinoma risk.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: A 24-year-old presents with several weeks of bloody diarrhoea with mucus, tenesmus and LLQ cramping pain. Colonoscopy shows continuous inflammation from the rectum with pseudopolyps, and biopsy shows crypt abscesses and goblet cell depletion. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: Ulcerative colitis
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: Bloody diarrhoea with mucus and tenesmus, continuous inflammation from the rectum with pseudopolyps, and crypt abscesses with goblet cell depletion on biopsy are all characteristic of UC.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: A 28-year-old smoker has chronic non-bloody diarrhoea, weight loss, RIF pain and perianal skin tags. MRI shows terminal ileal disease with a fistula, and biopsy shows granulomas. Which single statement best fits this case?
options: This is Crohn's disease; surgery would not be curative as disease recurs panenterically
This is ulcerative colitis; panproctocolectomy would be curative
Smoking is protective in this condition
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: This is Crohn's disease; surgery would not be curative as disease recurs panenterically
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: Non-bloody diarrhoea, weight loss, terminal ileal disease, perianal disease, fistula and granulomas indicate Crohn's. Smoking worsens Crohn's, and surgery is not curative because disease recurs at new sites (panenteric).

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: A patient with Crohn's affecting the terminal ileum is noted to have a macrocytic anaemia. Which nutritional deficiency is most likely responsible?
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: B12 deficiency
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: Malabsorption/nutritional complications in Crohn's include B12 deficiency (terminal ileum), fat-soluble vitamins, iron, folate and oxalate renal stones. Terminal ileal disease specifically impairs B12 absorption.

conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.question: A patient with long-standing UC develops anaemia. Which mechanisms are described as responsible?
options: B12 deficiency from terminal ileal disease
Folate deficiency from a gluten-free diet
Chronic blood loss (iron-deficiency) and anaemia of chronic disease (↑IL-6, ↓erythropoiesis)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.answer: Chronic blood loss (iron-deficiency) and anaemia of chronic disease (↑IL-6, ↓erythropoiesis)
conditions__LOWER GI & BOWEL__Inflammato.explanation: In UC, anaemia results from chronic blood loss leading to iron-deficiency anaemia, plus anaemia of chronic disease (↑IL-6, ↓erythropoiesis).
